IST8310 external compass showing inconsistency

nodes.label: IST8310 external compass showing inconsistency
nodes.content: A user is experiencing a recurring 'compass inconsistency' error with an IST8310 external compass on a Cube Orange, especially after rebooting.

nodes.label: Post by Karukkuvel0Killis describing the initial problem
nodes.content: Hi everyone, we integrated holybro micro m10 gps with ist8310 to cube orange, for which it showed compass inconsistency, which can be reset by changing the rotation parameters of mag. But again during rebooting, the same issue arises again, for that we need to again change the rotation parameters of mag. I think this issue arises for the controllers which don’t define the IST8310 as default external compass like that in px4 fmu-v6c. I tested it with my custom hardware, by omitting the ist8310 as external compass in the init/rc.board_sensors files, the firmware showed same compass inconsistency error as shown in the cubeorange. When including the ist8310 as default external compass in the init/rc.board_sensors file the compass works normally. P.S: We ensured the forward markings of both the gps and FC align in the same direction.

nodes.label: Post by Karukkuvel0Killis with the solution
nodes.content: Sensor issues were restored after the calibration. The issue is we didn’t accept the rotational values generated by the firmware after the calibration. We tried to resolve the issue by changing the rotation parameters manually which caused sensors inconsistency issue, every time we rebooted.

The drone won’t arm in altitude mode (though QGroundControl shows it’s armed), and the motors don’t spin. 2. In manual mode, the drone arms and the motors spin autonomously, but it can’t be controlled by the Jetson. 3. It won’t also arm on offboard mode because it says the required position data is missing. We suspect either a parameter reset or a communication issue between the Jetson and Cube Orange+. Any advice on resolving this?

graphs.title: Compass priority configuration results with Freefly RTK and Holybro F9P

nodes.label: Compass priority configuration results with Freefly RTK and Holybro F9P
nodes.content: A thread discussing the confusing results of testing compass priority configurations with Freefly RTK and Holybro F9P GPS/magnetometer modules.

nodes.label: Post by Ungravity_fpv sharing test results
nodes.content:
Hi! we did some test and wanted to share with the comunity since the results are quite confusing. We´d like to choose which is the best configuration (and hardware) based on this results:

Description:

stimulating with a magnet the two compasses (internal and external) we study the magnetic field variations depending on the priority settings.

we allways touch 3 times the external compass, and then, 3 times the internal one… allways i this exact order.

we test it with freefly gps/mag and with hollybro F9P (auterion) GPS/mag with the following results:

The results are a bit confusing, but we can extract some data:

It seems like the external sensor conditions the behavior of the internal one.

When priority is set to 50% we obserb different behavior.

Whith the freefly´s, the external sensor has priority over the internal (5u variations vs 0,2u). While with the holybro, is the opposite (internal varies 0,05u vs 11u variations in the internal)

When set to 100% external mag priority; it has the expected behavior, but magnitudes are different:

The freefly´s peak, is observed to 10u, while the holybro´s reaches just 3,5u, the internal one has also less magntude when setted with the holybro (0,05u vs 0,3u aprox with the freefly)

When set to 100% internal priority, we see the expected behavior, but again, the magnitude with the holybro, seems to be limmited for the internal:

The peak reaches 28u with the freefly, while just reaches 3.1u with the holybro.

We can just conclude that it seems like the Holybro gives an overall more atenuated signal. Magnetic field varies from 0 to 3.5u (except in 50% priority config)

I wait for your comments and conclussions if there´s one.

Thanks!

graphs.title: It took at least 1 minute to broadcast mavlink message on UDP

nodes.label: It took at least 1 minute to broadcast mavlink message on UDP
nodes.content: A user experiences a delay of at least 80 seconds before their computer receives MAVLink broadcast messages from a flight controller over a direct UDP Ethernet connection.

nodes.label: Post by dong_chen describing the MAVLink UDP delay issue
nodes.content:
Hi
I am using a single Ethernet cable to directly connect the computer and the flight controller.
I noticed that it will took at least 80s for the computer receive mavlink broadcast message.
the computer IPv4 is 192.168.0.10 Gateway is 192.168.0.254,
the Flight controller IPv4 is 192.168.0.3 Gateway is 192.168.0.245
software version : v1.14.3
hardware version : Holybro v6x pro

nsh> netman show
DEVICE=eth0
BOOTPROTO=fallback
NETMASK=255.255.255.0
IPADDR=192.168.0.3
ROUTER=192.168.0.254
DNS=192.168.0.254

when it haven’t ready , run command on the nsh: ifconfig

eth0    Link encap:Ethernet HWaddr 7a:64:e7:a9:46:ad at UP
         inet addr:0.0.0.0 DRaddr:192.168.0.254 Mask:255.255.255.0

when it ready, run command on the nsh: ifconfig

nsh> ifconfig   
eth0    Link encap:Ethernet HWaddr 7a:64:e7:a9:46:ad at UP
        inet addr:192.168.0.3 DRaddr:192.168.0.254 Mask:255.255.255.0

I don’t understand why it took so long for the ethernet to get ready.

nodes.label: Post by dong_chen providing the solution
nodes.content:
I solved the problem by set the BOOTPROTO=static
In the fallback mode, firstly it will wait for the dhcp sever to give ip address, then after 80s, it find it can’t get ip address from dhcp sever. then it will use the written ip address in the file.
The static option doesn’t have the problem. It will get the ip address firstly.

graphs.title: Toolchain Install: No module named 'em'

nodes.label: Toolchain Install: No module named 'em'
nodes.content: A user is unable to compile the PX4 toolchain on a new M3 MacBook running Sonoma due to a Python module import error, 'No module named em'. The root cause is identified as having multiple conflicting Python versions, and the solution is to use a virtual environment (venv) to manage dependencies with a single Python installation.

nodes.label: Post by John_Walls: Initial Problem Report
nodes.content:
Hi - I’m trying to set up the toolchain on a new (M3) MacBook running Sonoma.

I’ve followed the Mac instructions and run into this error when trying to compile:

On typing: make px4_sitl gazebo-classic

I get:
Failed to import em: No module named ‘em’

You may need to install it using:
pip3 install --user empy

I try and install empy and get ‘Requirement already satisfied’. Have tried PIP uninstall and reinstall: same issue. Have also tried some of the solutions for similar issues in the forum - but sudo solution doesn’t work for me.

Can anyone help?

John

nodes.label: Post by abisop: Suggests specific empy version
nodes.content:
Px4 requires the version i mentioned.
use : pip install empy==3.3.4
Note : dont use sudo…

To know if this is a path error maybe
Try manual importing em in python shell.

nodes.label: Post by John_Walls: Discovers multiple Python versions
nodes.content:
Further investigation - looks like the standard install has left me with 2 version of Python - v3.9.6 and v3.12

Am trying to use venv to manage access to right packages - not go there yet.

I can’t see the right version of python in the requirement.txt file - any recommendation before I try to uninstall one?

nodes.label: Post by John_Walls: Problem Solved
nodes.content:
Thanks Abhishek - I think the main setup and therefore the default instructions end up with 2 versions of python installed 3.9 and 3.12.

I cleared my .venv and set it up from scratch with a single python version (3.12) - seemed to clear the import not found error - which is a step forward.

Still not building cleanly but I’ll investigate that separately.

Really appreciate your help

nodes.label: Post by maya about drone inspection issues
nodes.content: I’m making a drone to automatically do inspections on trees to detect parasites growing on trees in remote forrests. The drone can fly to an infected spot on the tree, take a note about when/where, then dash to another tree in a hurry. Forrests are big. The object recognition system itself is complete, and I’ve managed to create a ROS2 topic that can subscribe to the running camera feed with bounding boxes. The drone does fly but has problems. It’s not responsive when it starts to chase a tree. It’s a little difficult to set/guess the tree’s waypoints based on geometry of the drone relative to the ground, the detected object, etc. What I really want is to fly to a detected tree object in the aperature of the camera. The problem I’ve noticed is getting the drone to respond to the bounding box moving around after the drone initially reacts. I’ll eventually make a PID controller but right now I’ve been depending on drone.offboard.set_velocity_body(VelocityBodyYawspeed(forward, left_right, down, yawspeed)) To get the drone to pitch up/down, left/right. forward is just set to 5.0. yawspeed is also constant but neg/pos depending on left_right’s value. I know I’m missing some important concept or abstraction to make the drone more responsive to the Bounding box moving in the camera. Could anyone offer any hints?

nodes.label: Post by JeSz
nodes.content: Provides answers to the questions. 1. Explains that vehicle_global_position is derived from the EKF's local position estimate, not directly from the raw GPS. 2. Confirms that vehicle_global_position refers to COG and vehicle_gps_position refers to the GPS antenna.

nodes.label: Post by Safranek42
nodes.content: Accepts the answer for the second question. For the first, clarifies the expectation that since the more accurate RTK GPS data is used in the fusion, the fused position's accuracy (eph, epv) should also improve, but it doesn't seem to.

nodes.label: Post by JeSz
nodes.content: Agrees that accuracy should increase with an RTK fix, but suggests it might take time for the EKF variances to settle.

nodes.label: Post by Safranek42

nodes.label: Post by Syed_Muhammad_Alam describing the setup and problem
nodes.content: I am using an indoor localization solution using UWB devices that provides me with x,y values and using range finder lidar for my vertical position. The UWB localization solution was computed on an onboard computer running ROS1 noetic and relayed to /mavros/vision_pose/pose topic. graphs.title: Unable to connect Raspberry Pi 4 to mRo Pixhawk flight controller via uXRCE-DDS wired serial connection

nodes.label: Unable to connect Raspberry Pi 4 to mRo Pixhawk flight controller via uXRCE-DDS wired serial connection
nodes.content: A user is unable to establish a uXRCE-DDS wired serial connection between a Raspberry Pi 4 and an mRo Pixhawk flight controller, despite following the official guide.

nodes.label: Post by Geol-23 detailing connection issues and troubleshooting steps
nodes.content:
Hello,
I’m using a Raspberry Pi 4 (Ubuntu 22.04) to communicate with an mRo Pixhawk ( PX4 1.14.3). I’ve followed the guide and installed the agent as a standalone on the Pi, I’ve used the reccommended baud rates and ports (921600, TELEM2 on the FC and UART0 on the Pi), I believe the pins and connections are the correct way around and the wire connections are solid. I’ve also added the dialout permissions and I ran lsof /dev/ttyAMA0 to check nothing else is running on that port.

To diagnose this I’ve tried to boot up a seperate FC (same version and firmware as the main FC) and the issue persists. I’ve established communication with the FC using mavproxy.py according to the guide. I’ve also used screen and minicom to take a look at the data going through /dev/ttyAMA0 when the FC and RPi are connected and there is activity (albeit it’s just invalid characters).

I think I’ve managed to narrow it down to a software issue on the Raspberry Pi. Using a feedback loop across the TX and RX pins on the Pi, I’ve managed to send and recieve characters over the serial port.

I’ve also tried installing the Agent as a ROS2 package and the issue still persits. To ensure that the workspace actually built I had to clone an earlier version of the MicroXRCE-DDS-Agent, 2.2.1. With the two devices disconnected and reading the voltage at the TX and RX pins on the Pi, both pins read 3.3V. I’m pretty sure the UART protocol is that the TX pin is high by default but would it matter if the RX pin 3.3V?

Also using screen or minicom and the same feedback loop as before, no characters appear on the terminal when running the agent. This tells me that the agent isn’t attempting to handshake with the with the client.

Logs

Raspberry Pi:

MicroXRCEAgent serial --dev /dev/ttyAMA0 -b 921600 -v 6
[1709157626.383849] info | TermiosAgentLinux.cpp | init | running... | fd: 3
[1709157626.385726] info | Root.cpp | set_verbose_level | logger setup | verbose_level: 6

Flight Controller

nsh> uxrce_dds_client status
INFO [uxrce_dds_client] Running, disconnected
INFO [uxrce_dds_client] Using transport: serial

To Reproduce

  1. Install the agent standalone the RPi and configure UART0 per the guide
  2. Configure the baud rate (921600), port (TELEM2) and leave everything else default
  3. Reboot FC as needed and power it through the micro-usb port to your ground station (I’m using QGroundControl)
  4. Assuming the two are wired together and since the client is already running on the FC start the agent using this command MicroXRCEAgent serial -b 921600 -D /dev/ttyAMA0 -v 6

Expected behavior

The guide states that there should be some output on the RPi terminal and the FC terminal but nothing changes for me. When I check the status of the client, it’s running but not connected. Same with the output on the terminal.

I’m still relatively new to the Pixhawk environment so any help is appreciated.
Cheers.

nodes.label: Post by Romain_Chiappinelli
nodes.content:
Hi all,

This is a side topic for those interested to know how many lines of code PX4 contains. I used cloc to count the lines of C/C++ code on PX4 release v1.14.0.

The command cloc . --include-lang=C++,C gives me 324666 lines of code

I first though, “yeaaah but Nuttx contains probably 90% of these lines of code”. So I ran it on the subdirectory src/modules and I obtained…

152346 lines of code!

Good job PX4 developers! I’m truly impressed!
A few other metrics on src/modules/

  • 14979 for ekf2
  • 10120 for the mavlink
  • 9824 for the commander
  • 6001 for the navigator
  • 4687 for the sensors
  • 3209 for the logger
  • 2536 for the flight_mode_manager
  • 2293 for fw_pos_control
  • 1382 for px4iofirmware
  • 1312 for mc_pos_control
  • 660 for the muorb
  • 515 for simulation/simulator_sih (big up to me)
  • 499 for fw_att_control
  • 395 for mc_att_control
  • 253 for mc_rate_control
  • 79689 for src/drivers

nodes.label: Thread: Heavy drone climbs unresponsively after takeoff in PX4 sitl gazebo
nodes.content: A discussion about a heavy drone (250kg) simulation in PX4 SITL Gazebo that exhibits an uncontrolled climb after takeoff, and the eventual solution.

nodes.label: Post by MostafaMGTech describing the initial problem
nodes.content: A custom 250kg coaxial octorotor UAV model in gazebo-classic sitl is able to takeoff, but a few seconds later it climbs unresponsively. This seems to be related to the motor constant values. The user lists the calculated motor parameters.

nodes.label: Post by MostafaMGTech with log file
nodes.content: Provides a log file showing the drone takes off at 30% RC throttle, is stable, but then climbs even when throttle is brought to zero. The unresponsive climb starts when the motor velocity and thrust jump.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes diagnosing the issue
nodes.content: Diagnoses the drone as 'way over-powered'. Observes that once thrust goes to the minimum (0.12), it keeps climbing.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes on Gazebo motor plugin
nodes.content: Suggests that the Gazebo motor plugin parameters are often not physically accurate and are usually tweaked by trial and error until hover thrust is around 50%.

nodes.label: Post by MostafaMGTech presenting the solution
nodes.content: Identifies the solution: the default values for the gazebo_mavlink_interface plugin (input_offset, input_scaling, etc.) in the sdf file were causing very small PWM signals for the powerful motors. Adjusting these values allowed for a 50% hover throttle.

nodes.label: Post by Khamethor with similar issue in Gazebo Harmonic
nodes.content: Reports the same uncontrolled climb issue but in the Gazebo Harmonic environment, which uses MicroXRCE instead of the MAVLink plugin, making the original solution inapplicable.

nodes.content: Describes an opposite problem in PX4 SITL and Gazebo Harmonic: a 50kg Octorotor fails to take off more than 1m when its weight is increased, suggesting a related but different parameter tuning issue.

nodes.label: Post by Unknown9190: Initial problem statement
nodes.content: User reports that after building and uploading PX4 firmware v1.14.2 for fmu-v2 onto a Pixhawk 3DR board, the uXRCE-related parameters are missing in QGroundControl v4.4.0. The goal is to use a telemetry radio to connect to ROS 2. Simulation works fine.

nodes.content: User discovers that a Pixhawk 2.4.8 board with fmu-v3 firmware works correctly and has the XRCE parameters, while the Pixhawk 2.4.6 board with fmu-v2 does not. Attempting to upload fmu-v3 firmware to the 2.4.6 board results in a 'Firmware image is too large' error.

nodes.label: Post by sibujacob: Hypothesis on memory constraints
nodes.content: Suggests that the Pixhawk 2.4.6 board (fmu-v2) may lack sufficient memory or CPU capacity for the uXRCE module. Proposes removing unwanted modules from the build to free up space.

nodes.label: Post by Unknown9190: Decision to upgrade hardware
nodes.content: The user agrees that memory limitations are the likely cause and decides that upgrading to a newer Pixhawk 2.4.8 board is a better solution than modifying the fmu-v3 firmware modules.

nodes.label: Post by Unknown9190: New problem with unstable connection
nodes.content: After setting up the new board, the user faces a new issue: the uXRCE connection over telemetry radio is very weak, laggy, and unstable. They have configured UXRCE_DDS_CFG on TELEM2 and disabled MAV_1_CONFIG.

nodes.label: Post by sibujacob: Suggestion to check baudrate
nodes.content: Suggests setting the TELEM2 baudrate to the highest possible value.

nodes.label: Post by Unknown9190: Solution for unstable connection
nodes.content: User confirms the baudrate is at its maximum (921600). The root cause was that the default uXRCE topic publish rates were too high for the telemetry radio's bandwidth. The issue was resolved by decreasing the frequency of unimportant topics and increasing desired ones.

nodes.label: Post by rroche: Definitive solution for original problem
nodes.content: Confirms that the uXRCE module is disabled by default on the fmu-v2 target due to flash constraints. Provides a definitive solution: enable the module for a custom build by adding 'CONFIG_MODULES_UXRCE_DDS_CLIENT=y' to the 'boards/px4/fmu-v2/default.px4board' file, while ensuring other modules are disabled to save space.

nodes.label: Post by monkescripts
nodes.content: User sets up Micro XRCE-DDS Agent & Client. The environment is a flight controller with no GPS connected to an Nvidia Jetson Orin Nx via ethernet. They can see topics with 'ros2 topic list' but cannot echo specific topics like /fmu/out/vehicle_local_position and /fmu/out/vehicle_status. A custom subscriber node also fails to trigger its callback. The user suspects it is not a px4_msgs version mismatch as they are using firmware release 1.14.3 and the latest px4_msgs from GitHub.

nodes.label: Post by Cole_Malinchock
nodes.content: Another user reports having the same issue with their NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano 8GB.

nodes.label: Post by monkescripts
nodes.content: The original poster reports they fixed the issue. It was a version mismatch between the flight controller firmware and the branch of px4_msgs they were using. They suggest debugging by comparing topic definitions in the MAVLink console (via QGC) against the message definitions in the px4_msgs branch.

nodes.label: Post by Jimi1811
nodes.content: A user reports the same issue while using PX4 Autopilot tag v1.14.3 and px4_msgs branch release/1.14. They are using Isaac ROS packages in Docker and can connect via DDS but see no topics.

nodes.label: Post by monkescripts
nodes.content: The original poster clarifies their solution: they directly copied the message definitions from the PX4-Autopilot repo under tag v1.14.3, rather than using the px4_msgs release/1.14 branch, to ensure an exact match.

nodes.label: Post by Cole_Malinchock
nodes.content: The second user confirms the solution worked. They copied the msg folder from the firmware release/1.14 into their px4_msgs workspace, removed the old one, and adjusted some message field names (e.g., latitude_deg to lat) in their listener code to resolve build errors.

nodes.label: Post by AlbertoJimenezUC3M

nodes.content: A thread discussing a significant RPM difference between clockwise (CW) and counter-clockwise (CCW) motors on a hexacopter, where CW motors work much harder than CCW motors.

nodes.label: Post by JeSz
nodes.content: Initial post describing the problem: CW motors are at 60% throttle while CCW motors are at 20%. The user has built a hexacopter with CubeOrange, T-Motors MN601-S, and 20-inch props. They have checked for mechanical imbalance and are holding off on PID tuning.

nodes.content: Another user reports a similar issue on a Quadcopter with CubeOrange running PX4 v1.13.3.

nodes.content: Specifies the firmware version as PX4 v1.14.3 and that the propellers are all identical T-Motor P20x6 CF.

nodes.label: Post by sibujacob
nodes.content: Suggests that the issue might be related to the Center of Gravity (CoG).

nodes.label: Post by nsr
nodes.content: Suggests that the cause could be one or more motors having a slight tilt around the mounting tube, creating a yaw force that needs to be compensated by differential thrust.

nodes.label: Post by TH8
nodes.content: Argues that a significant motor tilt (a 'corkscrew fashion' mounting) must be the cause, as otherwise the differential thrust would cause the craft to spin uncontrollably.

nodes.label: Post by TH8
nodes.content: Suggests a method to check for motor misalignment: attach long tubes to the motor shafts to make any misalignment visually apparent.

nodes.label: Post by JeSz
nodes.content: The final post confirming the solution. The user found that motor 4 was slightly tilted (0.5-1.0 degrees). Fixing the tilt resolved the RPM imbalance issue.

nodes.label: Initial post by Noe-Sanchez describing the problem
nodes.content: I built a drone usign the X500v2 kit and a Jetson Orin Nano back here at the lab, where we have a VICON system setup. Ive already made the necesary connections and configuration for the jetson, which is connected though the xrce-dds agent to the Pixhawk 6C, to see and receive the pose estimation at ~118 Hz. After publishing to the /fmu/in/vehicle_visual_odometry topic, with non-specified timestamp and timestamp_sample,  I have a pose reassembling the one from the VICON system, but a weird thing is happening, every 10 seconds or so, the topics relating to position and odometry dissappear, and I’ve noticed the EKF2 is not running as fast as without the vision aid, perhaps this could be related to the EKF2_EV_DELAY param? I decided to check on the shell the EKF2 status, and found out that the EKF2 is missing visual odometry events...

nodes.label: Post by Halil suggesting PID and vibration issues
nodes.content: Hi there, you have really bad vibration, which can be because of pid. But firstly check if sth may cause too much vibration. if you are using 2.4.8 pixhawk, use dampers. But I think the real issue about the pid, even in manual mode, if you check the motor outputs they are crazy, when you switch to position, since much more control is tried to be done, you see the effect of bad pid more clearly. I see that you have chosen generic quadcopter as your frame, firstly try to choose a specific airframe model more close to your frame. then bu sure that your drone flies somewhat better, then you can go for autotune I think. In the end your motor outputs shouldn’t oscillate much, it should be a thin line. also check the raw acceleration, yours is really bad, but most probably this is also caused by pids.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes

graphs.title: Time adjustment of data samples in obs buffer

nodes.label: Time adjustment of data samples in obs buffer
nodes.content: A thread discussing the reason and formula for time adjustment of sensor data samples before they are pushed to observation buffers in the EKF2 estimation system.

nodes.label: Question about time adjustment formula
nodes.content: I’m working on the estimation system and found that a time adjustement is performed to the sensor’s data samples before pushing them to their respective buffers using the formula: adjusted_timestamp = sensor_sample_time - EKF2_(sensor)_DELAY - ekf2_update_interval/2. What’s the reason behind performing this time adjustment and why this specific formula?

nodes.label: Follow-up post
nodes.content: Gentlemen any suggestions? @JulianOes, @Paul_Riseborough, @bresch

nodes.label: Explanation of the time adjustment
nodes.content: The formula is explained in two parts. First, `sensor_sample_time - EKF2_(sensor)_DELAY` gives the actual timestamp of the measurement by accounting for the delay between measurement and driver timestamping. Second, subtracting `ekf2_update_interval/2` is a technique to center the sample within the EKF update interval, minimizing the maximum time alignment error.

nodes.label: Sensor Timestamp Adjustment
nodes.content: The process of correcting a sensor sample's timestamp to account for system delays before it is used by the EKF.

nodes.label: EKF2 Module
nodes.content: The Extended Kalman Filter version 2 module, which is part of the estimation system and uses sensor data to estimate the vehicle's state.

nodes.label: Estimation System
nodes.content: The system responsible for state estimation, which includes the EKF2 module.

nodes.label: adjusted_timestamp
nodes.content: The final, corrected timestamp of a sensor sample before it is pushed to the observation buffer.

nodes.label: sensor_sample_time
nodes.content: The timestamp recorded by the sensor driver when the sample is received.

nodes.label: EKF2_(sensor)_DELAY
nodes.content: The expected delay between the actual physical measurement by the sensor and the timestamping performed by the driver.

nodes.label: ekf2_update_interval
nodes.content: The time interval between two consecutive updates of the EKF.

nodes.label: Explanation of Time Adjustment Formula
nodes.content: The time adjustment formula corrects for two types of delay: 1) The inherent delay between a sensor's physical measurement and its timestamping in the driver (`EKF2_(sensor)_DELAY`). 2) It minimizes time alignment error by centering the sample within an EKF update cycle (`ekf2_update_interval/2`), ensuring the maximum error is less than or equal to half the update interval.

nodes.label: Time Alignment Error
nodes.content: The error that occurs when a sensor measurement's timestamp does not align perfectly with the discrete update steps of the EKF.

graphs.title: Why use the uncorrected angular velocity in observation model

nodes.label: Why use the uncorrected angular velocity in observation model
nodes.content: A thread questioning the use of raw, uncorrected angular velocity for GPS velocity correction in the EKF2 observation model.

nodes.label: Post by hhenryy
nodes.content: If the GPS is mounted at an offset from the CoG, any angular velocity from the vehicle will induce a velocity due to the rotation, which is unwanted and needs to be corrected for. In the GPS measurement model, this is accounted for, by subtracting the induced velocity caused by the positional offset. However, the uncorrected raw angular velocity is used. What is the reason to use the uncorrected angular velocity?

nodes.label: hhenryy
nodes.content: The user who initiated the thread and asked the question.

nodes.label: GPS Velocity Correction Using Uncorrected Angular Velocity
nodes.content: The core topic is understanding the rationale behind using uncorrected (raw) angular velocity to calculate and compensate for the induced velocity at an offset GPS antenna within the EKF2's GPS measurement model.

nodes.label: EKF2 Module
nodes.content: The Extended Kalman Filter (EKF2) module in PX4-Autopilot responsible for state estimation. It uses a GPS measurement model to process GNSS data.

nodes.label: PX4-Autopilot
nodes.content: The open-source flight control software where the EKF2 module is implemented.

nodes.label: GPS Sensor
nodes.content: A Global Positioning System sensor mounted on the vehicle, typically at an offset from the IMU or Center of Gravity.

nodes.label: IMU Sensor
nodes.content: An Inertial Measurement Unit that provides raw angular rate and acceleration data.

nodes.label: Uncorrected Angular Velocity (_ang_rate_delayed_raw)
nodes.content: The raw angular velocity calculated directly from IMU delta angles over a time delta, without applying bias corrections. It is used to compute the velocity offset.

nodes.label: GPS Positional Offset
nodes.content: The physical vector distance (lever arm) between the GPS antenna and the IMU (_params.gps_pos_body - _params.imu_pos_body). This offset, combined with angular velocity, induces a velocity at the GPS antenna.

nodes.label: Induced Velocity
nodes.content: The velocity component at the GPS antenna's location caused by the vehicle's rotation around the IMU. It is calculated as the cross product of the angular velocity and the positional offset.

nodes.label: GPS Measurement Model
nodes.content: The model within the EKF that processes GPS velocity measurements. It corrects the observed GPS velocity by subtracting the induced velocity from the vehicle's rotation.

I am using px4_sitl in gazebo classic. thanks for the help

nodes.label: Explanation of position vs. velocity control by Jaeyoung-Lim
nodes.content: If you are sending zero velocity, you wont be able to control the position, since it is not controlling it. The tracking error of velocity would accumulate resulting in a drift. If you want the vehicle to keep position, you should control position, not velocity

nodes.label: Follow-up question on relative position control by shahar753
nodes.content: So if I want to hover I need to set position. Can I set position relative to the drone frame? (I want to set 0,0,0) I tried to use SET_POSITION_TARGET_LOCAL_NED but It only supports position that relative to the home of the drone.

nodes.label: Clarification on why relative frame control causes drift by Jaeyoung-Lim
nodes.content: No, because then it will be always moving (wherever the drone is it is 0, 0, 0) and will drift.

nodes.label: User confirms solution by shahar753
nodes.content: Ok thanks for the help I will use global frame (lat, long) to hold position.

nodes.content: Hi there! Sorry if in the wrong place - cant quite find a right category for this. So I’m trying to connect a receiver Blue MX SR3100 to the Kakute H7 V2. nodes.label: Post by riku.rusanen providing a solution
nodes.content: Thanks already, got this solved with ChagGPT 3.5. So it goes like this: To connect the Spektrum SR3100 receiver to the Kakute H7 V2 flight controller, you’ll typically use a UART... Connect the signal wire... to the chosen UART port on the Kakute H7 V2 flight controller... Connect the positive (+) and negative (-) wires... to an appropriate power source... configure the Kakute H7 V2 flight controller to recognize and communicate with the SR3100 receiver... And for the last advice the ChatGPT told me to use UART RX pins for the job.

nodes.label: Post by luois asking for PX4 documentation for SIYI camera
nodes.content: I want to connect my SIYI camera module with my Flight controller. I know ardupilot has some drivers to do the same job. How can I do this using px4? I can’t find any documentation regarding this.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes suggesting a Raspberry Pi based solution
nodes.content: I used a RPi with it, see: GitHub - julianoes/siyi-a8-mini-camera-manager: Camera Manager for SIYI A8 mini for RPi based on MAVSDK. The gimbal (with latest firmware) talks MAVLink gimbal v2 which PX4 understands, however, unfortunately you need to set a MAVLink param of the gimbal each time it is started up to enable it. For this, you have to connect the gimbal over serial and make sure the port is set to Forwarding On, so QGC can talk directly to the gimbal.

nodes.label: Post by hamishwillee on improving PX4 camera documentation
nodes.content: The whole camera section on PX4 is very “thin” - or more specifically it talks about the driver settings but is of little practical use if you want to connect a camera... We should fix that by at least linking to examples like this... My understanding here is that the linked repo builds a camera manager for the siyi-a8-mini-camera using MAVSDK server plugin... The camera gets connected to the RPi Ethernet... We also connect the RPi to Pixhawk and set up PX4 to use that port for MAVLink.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes clarifying solution details and documentation concerns
nodes.content: Confirms the setup details. Mentions the firmware used for testing was unreleased and the current official one has an annoying MAVLink param requirement. Expresses concerns about duplicating documentation and prefers linking to his repository to avoid maintenance overhead.

nodes.label: Post by luois asking about cross-platform compatibility
nodes.content: That is quite helpful but the SIYI camera manager is only for linux, right? Can’t we have something that can work as a cross platform?

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes clarifying MAVSDK is cross-platform
nodes.content: The camera manager is on top of MAVSDK which is cross platform. What are you thinking, Windows? Or do you mean embedded?

nodes.label: Post by oldgazer suggesting an alternative all-in-one solution
nodes.content: The easiest way I found for using an SiYi A8 camera/gimbal is going all in with an SiYi Enterprise MK32E Handheld GCS and HDMI Air Unit combo.

nodes.label: Initial Post by josh8991

nodes.label: Solution Post by josh8991
nodes.content: User discovered that installing an older PX4 version (1.13) for FMUv2 made the SYS_BL_UPDATE parameter accessible, allowing them to proceed with the bootloader update.

nodes.label: Clarification by hamishwillee

nodes.label: VTOL Quad Tailsitter Airframe & setup
nodes.content: A thread discussing the setup, configuration, and flight testing of a VTOL Quad Tailsitter using PX4 firmware.

nodes.label: Post by RaMansell on 2024-04-09
nodes.content: I’m building a VTOL Quad Tailsitter. It seems like there used to be a SYS_AUTOSTART = 13003 that would be used for Quad Tailsitters. That option doesn’t seem to exist anymore (PX4 1.14.0). How should we setup for a VTOL Quad Tailsitter in PX4 1.14.0? Would be like the following? 1. Under Airframes: select the “Generic VTOL Tailsitter” Airframe (SYS_AUTOSTART = 13200) 2. Under Actuators: select “4” from the MC Motors drop down menu 3. Under Actuators: input the X & Y offsets of the 4 motors 4. Under Actuators: make sure motors 1 & 2 do have “CCW” selected but motors 3 & 4 do not have “CCW” selected

nodes.label: Post by Simone_Ciresa on 2024-04-11
nodes.content: Yes, that seems to be correct. Then if you have control surfaces just add them in the same window. In case you don’t have any of them and rely just on differential thrust to control attitude, make sure to set CA_SV_CS_COUNT = 0 and VT_FW_DIFTHR_EN depending on your needs ( probably it will be set to 7 which is for the case you control all three angles with diff thrust)

nodes.label: Post by RaMansell on 2024-04-15
nodes.content: Test flight with the aforementioned parameters worked great! I had been trying to hover a quad motor Tailsitter with the 4 motors inline, but didn’t have enough control authority in Pitch with just the elevons. By offsetting the motors so that two were X+ direction and two were in the X- direction (as opposed to all inline) and then using the new parameters resulted in proper flight and hovering in “tailsitter” mode. Next we will work on transitioning to fixed wing flight mode.

nodes.label: Post by RaMansell on 2024-04-30
nodes.content: We have not attempted transition yet. We are currently working on dialing in the PID for hovering in multi-copter mode. Pitch and Yaw were easy, but Roll was the most off–probably because of having the four motors strung out along the wing like it is. No airspeed sensor yet. It will be installed before we start attempting transitioning to fixed wing mode.

nodes.label: Post by RaMansell on 2024-09-30
nodes.content: We used an “X” configuration: Motors 1 & 2 = CCW, Motors 3 & 4 = CW. Motor layout was just like the “Standard VTOL” airframe. The only difference is that since ours was a tailsitter, the belly of the plane was toward the 1 & 3 motors and the top of the plane was toward the 2 & 4 motors.

nodes.label: Post by Shivaprasad.Jali on 2024-10-01
nodes.content: I am also working on PX4 Quad Rotor tail sitter. My setup: Firmware: PX4 V1.14.3, Airframe: Generic VTOL Tailsitter, Airframe geometry: Tandom wing, Propulsion: 5008 400KV motor with 16" props (6S setup), Control surface: 4 elevon with differential thrust for Pitch and Yaw for FW. We were able to tune the multi-copter... We have done couple of FW transition, but the result was not fruitful.

nodes.label: Post by Farkhod_Khikmatov on 2024-10-04
nodes.content: Yes I have had multiple flights. Mine is for a company I can’t send a photo but we had very much hard time transitioning in the beginning due to airspeed requirements.

nodes.label: Post by Sunlight on 2024-12-24
nodes.content: I am a newer to VTOL，which comfused me a lot is how to install the Pixhawk flight control system of tailsitter？...if the Pixhawk Flight Controller is fixed in the Multicopter Frame or along the Fixed Wing Head Direction? And if I need to set the PX4 Param 'SENS_BOARD_ROT' to switch the FMU direction?

nodes.label: Post by bryie describing position estimation issue
nodes.content:
Hi all,

I’m working on a project that requires me to use offboard control for a quadcopter indoors, and the only sensors I have available are an ARKFLOW sensor and the sensors included inside of a Pixhawk 6X. For my project, I would like to send position commands via ROS2, and I have tested this so far by starting up ROS2 on the drone and echoing the local position topic as I move it around. Whenever I do this, I see that the z-coordinate is changing based on the reading obtained from the ARKFLOW range finder; however, the x and y coordinates only change as the drone is moving, and soon reset to near 0 once I stop moving it. Are there any parameters that I can change on QGroundControl so that I can use the optical flow to also obtain horizontal position estimates?

edit: after looking through the forum and seeing posts asking similar questions, it seems like an optical flow sensor isn’t enough to use position control offboard. In that case, can I still do velocity control by publishing a TrajectorySetpoint message with only the velocity field filled out?

graphs.title: Offboard Control via target position/attitude setpoints

nodes.label: Offboard Control via target position/attitude setpoints
nodes.content: A thread discussing issues with offboard control setpoint frequencies in PX4, which turned out to be a logging configuration misunderstanding.

nodes.label: Initial query on offboard control and uORB topic rates
nodes.content: User jmltorch is trying to use offboard control with attitude setpoints on a PX4 drone. They observe that their 30 Hz trajectory setpoints seem to be published internally to the position controller at only 5 Hz, based on log data. They ask about the underlying uORB structure, which module handles MAVLink commands, and if the internal broadcast rates for topics like trajectory_setpoint can be controlled.

nodes.label: Suggestion to check MAVLink bandwidth settings
nodes.content: User coolvision suggests the limitation is not uORB publishing, as the mavlink_receiver loop runs at 100Hz. They propose the issue might be related to MAVLink bandwidth settings and recommend checking the MAV_0_RATE parameter. They also state that higher setpoint frequencies (30Hz vs 10Hz) might not make a practical difference due to PID smoothing.

nodes.label: Problem resolution: It was a logging issue
nodes.content: User jmltorch confirms the problem was a misunderstanding. The default logging settings were limiting the uORB subscription rates for the logged topics, making the control frequencies appear lower than they actually were. The 30 Hz trajectory setpoints were being processed correctly.

nodes.label: Post by Lincolndrone
nodes.content: Hello community. I am trying to use only imu, barometer, and magnetic compass for offboard control. I want the odometry information to from these sensors only. How to achieve that? It seems that I have to use either gps, vision-inertial sensors, or optical flow to switch to the offboard mode. However, if I use these sensors, many times it outputs no reliable position estimates and refuse offboard switch. My application does not require precise localization. Thank you in advance!

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: Have you seen this? [link to ECL EKF tuning guide] I expect you will have to tune some of the estimator thresholds.

nodes.label: Post by Lincolndrone
nodes.content: Hi Julian, Thank you very much for your reply. We also check the offboard documentation page. It says it needs  position or pose/attitude information - e.g. GPS, optical flow, visual-inertial odometry, mocap, etc. Does this mean if we only use IMU, barometer and magenetic compass, it will not be able to switch to offboard. Indeed, we will use thrust and altitude control and will not send “set position” command.

nodes.label: Post by hamishwillee
nodes.content: You should be fine without GPS if you aren’t setting position commands - that’s what “OR” means above. FYI, the conditions for switching to offboard (and other modes) are listed here in the source: [link to mode_requirements.cpp] - as you can see you need your attitude, angular velocity and a steady stream of offboard points. That means IMU and maybe compass are probably the only absolute requirement from a mode switching point of view.

nodes.label: Post by Burhan describing the problem
nodes.content: The user details the steps taken to create a new `rc_cessna_mono_cam` model by modifying the `rc_cessna` model. These steps include creating new model and airframe files. When trying to build and run the simulation, an error occurs indicating that the `model.sdf` file cannot be found.

nodes.label: Post by Benja providing the solution
nodes.content: Another user explains that the issue is caused by the model directory (`Tools/simulation/gz`) being a git submodule. Running `make distclean` clears the submodule, deleting the newly created model files. The solution is to avoid `make distclean`, re-create the model, and force a full rebuild by removing the `build/` directory.

graphs.title: Multi EKF disaster

nodes.label: Multi EKF disaster
nodes.content: A user reports a quadcopter crash after the PX4 flight controller, running multiple EKF instances for sensor redundancy, switched to a faulty instance that had inconsistent data (e.g., estimating a 180-degree roll).

nodes.label: Post by g.mena
nodes.content: We were flying a quadcopter with a Cube Orange FMU. PX4 detected redundant IMUs (3) and Magnetometers (2) and started multiple EKF instances (6). During a flight one of the instances had the IMU with values totally inconsistent (for example estimating a roll of 180 deg). Despite that PX4 decided to switch to that instance making the quadcopter flip and ruinously fall down. How is it possible that PX4 decided to use an EKF instance that was completely far from the other 4 (that were insted aligned)? How is it possible that PX4, while in stable hovering, decided to switch to an EKF instance that was assuming the drone was upside down?!? I am stunned…there is still a huge gap from being a reliable system. If there is no control over several EKF instances probably this functionality should be disabled by default and with clear warnings.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: I’m sorry for the crash. That doesn’t sound good at all indeed. Can you tell me which PX4 version this was and please upload the log of the flight to logs.px4.io, and share here (or DM if need be). I can then have a closer look

nodes.label: Post by g.mena
nodes.content: Hi Julian, thanks for your answer. I just uploaded log here https://logs.px4.io/plot_app?log=e79075a4-d192-4128-a392-cc492cb06ef4. Firmware version was 1.13.3

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: Thanks for the log. This does indeed look a bit strange in terms of multiple EKFs. I don’t quite understand why it switched multiple times like this. I’m tagging @bresch hoping that he can have a quick look at the log. He might also be aware of fixes that have been made since v1.13.3 to address this.

nodes.label: Post by thomas-ma
nodes.content: any news on that issue? We are about to use multi EKF in 1.14 to gain better sensor error handling. However, reading this is not really re-assuring to use multi EKF.

Velocity and Position Control in Offboard Mode

nodes.label: Velocity and Position Control in Offboard Mode
nodes.content: A user is trying to control a standard VTOL in SITL using Offboard mode via MicroDDS. The drone will not exceed 7.7 m/s, which is below the required speed for transitioning to fixed-wing mode (10 m/s). The user is sending separate TrajectorySetpoint messages for position and velocity.

nodes.label: User's initial problem description
nodes.content: The user details their environment (Ubuntu 22.04, PX4 v1.14.2, MicroDDS, SITL, Gazebo) and the problem: a VTOL is speed-limited to 7.7 m/s in offboard mode, preventing transition to fixed-wing. They are using TrajectorySetpoint messages and have included their Python code which sends separate position and velocity setpoints.

nodes.label: Expert suggestion on TrajectorySetpoint usage
nodes.content: A user suggests that sending separate position and velocity setpoints is incorrect. They recommend sending a single TrajectorySetpoint message with both position (as a reference) and velocity (as a feedforward) fields populated. They also point out a potential yaw control conflict in the user's code which could saturate the rate controllers.

nodes.label: User confirms the solution worked
nodes.content: The original poster confirms that the suggestion worked. They note a small issue where velocity was not controlled when using a single message and defaulted to parameter values, but they are satisfied with the outcome.

nodes.label: QGroundControl HITL Airframe Motor doesn't spin
nodes.content: A thread discussing why motors do not spin in a Hardware-in-the-Loop (HITL) simulation setup using QGroundControl and PX4, especially when specific airframes or firmware versions are used.

nodes.label: Post by seemsgroup (Initial Problem)
nodes.content: My motors in Actuators will start spinning when I select Generic Quadcopter Airframe but when I choose HIL Quadcopter X Airframe, the motors won’t spin when I tried testing it. I’m also able to arm but nothing moves when the throttle is pushed up.

nodes.label: Post by Vacoff (Points to GitHub Issue)
nodes.content: Provides a link to a GitHub issue that describes a similar problem with HITL motor spinning in PX4 v1.14.0.

nodes.label: Post by Vacoff (Explains Cause and Solution)
nodes.content: Confirms the issue is due to insufficient memory for all modules in PX4 v1.14. Suggests that it should work on v1.13 and recommends resetting all parameters after a firmware change.

nodes.label: Post by seemsgroup (Discovers Workaround)
nodes.content: Discovered that the issue is related to the 'HITL enabled' setting under the safety section. Disabling it allows the motors to move.

nodes.label: Post by Behnoush (Similar Issue, Different Setup)
nodes.content: Reports a similar issue of being unable to arm in HITL using Pixhawk 6C, PX4 1.14.3, Gazebo 11.10.2, and the Holybro X500 V2 airframe.

nodes.label: Post by idan_fiksel1 (Detailed Investigation)
nodes.content: Investigates the difference between 'HITL enable' and 'external HITL' on a Cube Orange with v1.13.3. Found that adding 'CONFIG_MODULES_SIMULATION_PWM_OUT_SIM=y' allows IRL motor control when 'external HITL' is set.

graphs.title: Control allocation roll/pitch torque effectiveness actual meaning

nodes.label: Control allocation roll/pitch torque effectiveness actual meaning
nodes.content: A thread discussing the meaning of roll/pitch torque effectiveness values within PX4's control allocation system, using a paramotor and flying wing as examples.

nodes.label: Initial query on torque effectiveness
nodes.content: User junwoo0914 asks for clarification on the meaning of 'roll/pitch torque values' in the actuator configuration for a paramotor system. They use a flying wing with two elevons as an example to question whether the absolute or relative values of effectiveness matter.

nodes.label: Theoretical explanation of control allocation
nodes.content: User hhenryy explains that the effectiveness values are elements of a control effectiveness matrix (F), which relates actuator deflections to the torques they generate. This matrix is then inverted (using a pseudo-inverse) to create a control allocation matrix (F^-1) that maps desired torques to the required actuator deflections. The values are normalized relative to the most effective surface for a given axis.

nodes.label: Follow-up questions on normalization
nodes.content: User junwoo0914 asks follow-up questions about how the absolute scale of actuator deflection is determined and about the normalization factor, suspecting it relates to the maximum combined torque of all actuators. A related GitHub issue on normalization is linked.

nodes.label: Detailed explanation with matrices
nodes.content: User hhenryy provides a more detailed answer showing how an unnormalized effectiveness matrix is derived from physical equations and then normalized. This normalized matrix is what is entered in QGC. PX4 then calculates the pseudo-inverse to get the control allocation matrix.

nodes.label: Query on servo torque scaling
nodes.content: User Iarlaith asks how PX4 converts a torque setpoint (e.g., 1Nm) into a specific servo deflection if there are no explicit parameters for the physical torque or moment coefficients for control surfaces, unlike for motors which have a thrust coefficient.

nodes.label: Control Allocation
nodes.content: The process of distributing a desired overall torque and thrust command from a controller among individual actuators (e.g., motors, control surfaces).

nodes.label: Torque Effectiveness
nodes.content: A normalized value representing how effective a single actuator's deflection is at generating torque around a specific axis (roll, pitch, yaw).

nodes.label: Control Effectiveness Matrix
nodes.content: A matrix whose elements represent the torque effectiveness of each actuator for each control axis (roll, pitch, yaw). It maps actuator commands to resulting torques.

nodes.label: Control Allocation Matrix
nodes.content: The inverse (or pseudo-inverse) of the control effectiveness matrix. It maps desired torques from the controller to the required actuator commands.

nodes.label: Normalization
nodes.content: The process of scaling the control effectiveness values, typically relative to the actuator that produces the largest torque in a given axis, so that the maximum effectiveness is 1.0.

nodes.label: Pseudo Inverse
nodes.content: A mathematical operation used to find the inverse of a non-square matrix, used here to derive the control allocation matrix from the control effectiveness matrix.

nodes.content: The open-source flight control software being discussed.

nodes.content: Control surfaces on a flying wing that combine the function of elevators (for pitch) and ailerons (for roll).

nodes.label: Servo
nodes.content: Actuators used to move control surfaces like elevons.

nodes.label: Roll/Pitch/Yaw Torque Effectiveness Values
nodes.content: The configurable parameters in PX4 that define the elements of the control effectiveness matrix for each actuator.

nodes.label: CA_SV_CS0_TRQ_P
nodes.content: A specific PX4 parameter for the pitch torque scaling of the first control surface (CS0).

nodes.label: Explanation of Torque Effectiveness
nodes.content: The torque effectiveness values entered by the user form a normalized Control Effectiveness Matrix. PX4 calculates the pseudo-inverse of this matrix to get a Control Allocation Matrix. This final matrix is used to translate the controller's desired roll, pitch, and yaw torque commands into specific deflection commands for each actuator (servo).

graphs.title: Adding Automatic Configuration Bypass to GPS Module

nodes.label: Adding Automatic Configuration Bypass to GPS Module
nodes.content: A thread discussing the addition of a feature to bypass the automatic configuration of GPS modules in PX4.

nodes.label: Post by thomasfrans on 2024-02-27
nodes.content:
Hi, I’m working as an intern at Septentrio. We wanted to add a feature to disable automatic GPS receiver setup. This would allow users to keep their receiver configuration and set up their data streams manually with a single parameter, without having to disable all GPS parameters in PX4 individually, which can help during testing or for advanced users. I was wondering whether this feature would be accepted.

In case it would, I also wanted to ask where this should be implemented. Is it something that goes in the PX4/PX4-GPSDrivers repository or should it live in the PX4/PX4-Autopilot one. I feel like it would make more sense in the autopilot code as the drivers themselves don’t “know” about automatic configuration. It’s up to the user of the driver to invoke the GPSHelper::configure() function. This would however require some changes in the drivers as not calling the configure() function will break some of them (for example the SBF driver).

A similar question was asked before on the forums, but that one was about the baud rate specifically. This one is about all of the automatic configuration/setup.

nodes.label: Post by fasdf detailing MAVLink shell connection issue in WSL2
nodes.content:
I am having trouble with the command

Tools/mavlink_shell.py 0.0.0.0:14550 -b 921600

in my WSL2.

I am connecting my Windows 11 laptop with Pixracer board over Wifi using ESP8266. All of my development code is in WSL2. Since WSL2 is essentially a virtual machine, it needs a special way to connect to Window’s Wifi... The following command should route the Windows Wifi connection to the port of my choice in WSL2:

netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenport=<yourPortToForward> listenaddress=0.0.0.0 connectport=<yourPortToConnectToInWSL> connectaddress=(wsl hostname -I) 

In WSL2, my ip address is 192.168.245.200... Thus, I did the following command in Powershell (run as Admin):

netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenport=14550 listenaddress=0.0.0.0 connectport=14550 connectaddress=192.168.245.200

which I understand is to listen port 14550 from any ip address on Windows 11 and send it to WSL2 on port 14550.

However when I run the following command in WSL2, it prints “Connecting to MAVLINK…”, but never establishes connection and I cannot use the shell.

(base) WSL2:~/PX4-Autopilot (main)$ Tools/mavlink_shell.py 0.0.0.0:14550 -b 921600

Any help would be greatly appreciated!

nodes.label: Unable to detect Pixhawk 6C Mini Flight Controller in Windows Device Manager and QGroundControl
nodes.content: A user is unable to get their Pixhawk 6C Mini detected by Windows Device Manager and QGroundControl after using usbipd to share the device with WSL.

nodes.label: Post by melc on 2024-02-18
nodes.content: Describes the initial problem where the Pixhawk 6C mini is no longer detected as a COM port in Windows and QGC after being used with WSL via usbipd commands. The device is still detectable by usbipd and in a Linux environment.

nodes.label: Post by melc on 2024-02-20
nodes.content: An update identifying a Windows driver issue where the FCU was stuck as a 'USBIP shared device'. After updating the driver, it's detected as a COM port again, but QGC still shows 'Disconnected' despite MAVLink messages being received. Suggests a possible firmware issue as ArduPilot works.

nodes.label: Post by melc on 2024-02-22
nodes.content: Further investigation reveals via MAVLink Inspector that the Component ID is 25 (MAV_COMP_ID_USER1) instead of the expected 1 for an autopilot.

nodes.label: Post by melc on 2024-04-24
nodes.content: The final solution is confirmed: the Component ID being 25 was the cause. Changing it back to 1 resolved the detection issue in QGC. The post notes that reflashing PX4 firmware didn't fix the ID, but flashing ArduPilot did.

nodes.content: Identifies the airspeed sensor as the mRo I2C Airspeed Sensor (MS4525DO).

nodes.label: Post by sfuhrer
nodes.content: Suggests that the low logging frequency (5Hz) might be missing the airspeed spike that triggers the transition and recommends increasing the logging rate.

nodes.label: Post by AWilkins_Ascend
nodes.content: Reports that activating the pusher motor for forward flight caused the UAV to immediately lose altitude, suspecting a power issue.

nodes.label: Post by sfuhrer
nodes.content: Analyzes that the multicopter system becomes unstable and motors saturate when the pusher starts. Suggests validating MC tuning and reducing VT_FWD_THRUST_SC. Considers power issues the most likely cause.

nodes.label: Post by AWilkins_Ascend
nodes.content: Concludes the problem was a damaged power module, likely from a previous crash. This was confirmed by enabling the pusher in MC mode (using VT_FWD_THRUST_EN), which caused the UAV to fail.

We should implement a histogram that keeps track of airspeed over time, and uses that to decide when a transition has finished (not just a small sample).

nodes.label: Post by Noah_Bruckner about documentation contradiction
nodes.content:
Hello. I am trying to develop a fixed-wing autonomous drone and use a raspberry pi as an offboard computer to control it. I have read the PX4 documentation on offboard computing as well as the MAVSDK documentation and have found some contradictory information. On the PX4 documentation, it says the following MAVLink commands are supported:
SET_POSITION_TARGET_LOCAL_NED
SET_POSITION_TARGET_GLOBAL_INT
SET_ATTITUDE_TARGET
MAV_CMD_DO_CHANGE_SPEED

However, the MAVSDK documentation says “The API uses the PX4 Offboard flight mode. The class can only be used with copter and VTOL vehicles (not fixed wing - a PX4 limitation) and currently only supports velocity setpoint commands (PX4 additionally supports position and thrust setpoints)”. Implying that no Fixed-Wing offboard commands are supported.

I am curious which documentation I should be following, as well as if there are any examples on controlling a fixed-wing drone with these commands. Thank you.

graphs.title: The large propeller coaxial octocopter crashed

nodes.label: The large propeller coaxial octocopter crashed
nodes.content: A user is seeking help after their large coaxial octocopter crashed immediately after takeoff. The thread discusses potential causes including PID tuning, actuator saturation, power issues, and vibrations.

nodes.label: Post by batu1881: Initial Crash Report
nodes.content: I have a large coaxial octocopter. I have 28-inch propellers, and I entered the frame type as ‘Generic 10" Octo coaxial geometry.’ I positioned the autopilot on the drone’s nose. Motor directions and connections are correct. The drone started to wobble from the moment it took off, and approximately 3-4 seconds later, it couldn’t be controlled, resulting in a crash. I am sharing my log.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes: Suggests Tuning Issue
nodes.content: Looks like the tuning did not translate to the big drone that you tried to fly. I would try to do some first tuning tests with the drone suspended using a rope and a kill switch on RC ready to switch off once it starts oscillating. Then you’ll have to slowly try to tune it in stabilized mode.

nodes.label: Post by batu1881: Drone Specs and Constraints
nodes.content: Our drone has a maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) of 48 kg with a 10 kg payload. It closely resembles the mentioned drone. Unfortunately, tethering is not an option for us. What alternative approaches can we consider?

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes: Alternative Tuning Method
nodes.content: Try to do very cautiously small hops in stabilized mode while doing the first tuning steps.

nodes.label: Post by terrymao886: Suggests Actuator Saturation
nodes.content: I think so that the actuators have overed 2000 is the main reason.

nodes.label: Post by batu1881: Second Flight Attempt
nodes.content: I have set my Proportional (P), Integral (I), and Derivative (D) coefficients to low values. In my second flight, I attempted to fly in stabilize mode, but the outcome was not as expected. Experiencing continuous disturbances during the tuning process should not be normal.

nodes.label: Post by terrymao886: Suggests Power Issue
nodes.content: Points to a log graph showing a potential power supply issue as the key problem.

nodes.label: Post by batu1881: Power System Description
nodes.content: what is wrong with it? i did not supply cube orange direct from battery there are 2 converters .1st one is 48v to 24 v .second one is cube orange step down module

nodes.label: Post by batu1881: Third Flight Attempt
nodes.content: Today’s flight was in altitude mode with the gain values I shared earlier. This time, I didn’t crash, but it still needs optimization. What approach should I take regarding my PID values

nodes.label: Post by Dhruvil: Suggests Vibration Issue

graphs.title: Problem with the formula for quaternion rotation in PX4

nodes.label: Problem with the formula for quaternion rotation in PX4
nodes.content: A discussion about a perceived discrepancy between standard quaternion rotation formulas and their implementation in the PX4 autopilot software, specifically concerning coordinate system transformations.

nodes.label: Post by zhihao: Initial query about quaternion formula discrepancy
nodes.content: User zhihao points out a conflict between their understanding of quaternion formulas for vector rotation (p’=qpq^-1) and coordinate system rotation (p’=q^-1pq), and the formula used in PX4's Quaternion.hpp (v_n = q_nb * [0;v_b] * q_nb^(-1)) for coordinate transformation.

nodes.label: Post by rmselvan: Mathematical explanation of the formula
nodes.content: User rmselvan explains that both formulas are applicable depending on which vector is being transformed. The PX4 formula transforms a vector from frame 'b' to 'n', and its algebraic manipulation results in the other formula, which transforms a vector from 'n' to 'b'.

nodes.label: Post by zhihao: Counter-argument and experimental findings
nodes.content: User zhihao remains unconvinced and presents findings from a fixed-wing aircraft test, suggesting that the quaternion `q` in the `vehicle_attitude` topic, though commented as FRD-to-NED, actually represents a NED-to-FRD transformation, creating a 'two negatives make a positive' situation.

nodes.label: Post by rmselvan: Proposing a negative angle convention
nodes.content: User rmselvan suggests the discrepancy might stem from the definition of the rotation angle, proposing that PX4 might be using a -2θ angle convention, which would make the formula `v_n = q_nb * v_b * q_nb^-1` correct. Also distinguishes between Direction-Cosine Matrix (DCM) and Rotation Matrix.

nodes.label: Post by zhihao: Pointing to quaternion initialization code
nodes.content: User zhihao directs the discussion to the `attitude_estimator_q_main.cpp` file, specifically the `init_attq()` function, where the attitude quaternion `_q` is initialized from a DCM, as a key piece of evidence.

nodes.label: Post by zhihao: Final conclusion before developer input
nodes.content: User zhihao concludes that PX4 uses a formula that appears incorrect for its stated purpose, and the only explanation is that the quaternion `q_nb` is mislabeled in comments and is actually `q_bn` (NED to FRD).

nodes.label: Post by bresch: Authoritative answer from PX4 developer
nodes.content: User bresch, a developer, provides the definitive answer, stating that PX4 uses the Hamilton convention for quaternions, and provides a reference paper showing the exact formula `v_n = q_nb * v_b * q_nb^-1` is correct under this convention for coordinate transformation.

nodes.label: Quaternion Formula Discrepancy
nodes.content: The core issue of the thread: PX4's formula for coordinate system rotation using quaternions appears to be the one typically used for active vector rotation, causing confusion.

nodes.label: p' = q⁻¹pq
nodes.content: The standard formula for rotating a coordinate system, where p' is the vector in the new coordinate system.

nodes.label: p' = qpq⁻¹
nodes.content: The standard formula for actively rotating a vector p by quaternion q.

nodes.label: v_n = q_nb * v_b * q_nb⁻¹
nodes.content: The specific formula implemented in PX4 to transform a vector from the body frame (b) to the navigation frame (n).

nodes.label: Direction-Cosine Matrix (DCM)
nodes.content: A matrix used to represent the orientation of one coordinate frame with respect to another. It is used in PX4 to initialize the attitude quaternion.

nodes.label: Quaternion.hpp
nodes.content: The PX4 library file (src/lib/matrix/matrix/Quaternion.hpp) that defines quaternion operations, including the `conjugate` function for vector rotation.

nodes.label: attitude_estimator_q_main.cpp
nodes.content: The PX4 module responsible for attitude estimation, containing the `init_attq()` function that initializes the attitude quaternion from a DCM.

nodes.label: init_attq()
nodes.content: A function in `attitude_estimator_q_main.cpp` that constructs a DCM from accelerometer and magnetometer data and converts it to an initial attitude quaternion.

nodes.label: PX4 uses the Hamilton Convention
nodes.content: The definitive solution is that PX4 adheres to the Hamilton convention, where the formula v_n = q_nb * v_b * q_nb⁻¹ is the correct representation for a passive coordinate system transformation from frame 'b' to frame 'n'.

graphs.title: About normalized torque and thrust in offboard control mode (ROS2 SITL)

nodes.label: About normalized torque and thrust in offboard control mode (ROS2 SITL)
nodes.content: A thread discussing the calculation and application of normalized thrust and torque for a quadrotor in a ROS2 SITL environment, and a subsequent issue with control instability.

nodes.label: Post by Hinoki: Initial question on normalization
nodes.content: User asks how to calculate normalized torque and questions why the observed normalized thrust for hovering (0.470) seems much higher than required for the drone's mass (1.0643 kg).

nodes.label: Post by Hinoki: Provides solution and raises new issue

nodes.content: User suggests that the control instability might be due to high CPU load rather than sensor noise, as the noise is typically not large enough to cause instability.

nodes.content: The control mode being used, where commands (like thrust and torque) are sent from an external computer (e.g., running ROS2).

nodes.content: A control input that is supposed to be normalized thrust, but is discovered to be normalized motor velocity.

nodes.content: A control input for the desired torque, which needs to be normalized.

nodes.label: Motor Constant
nodes.content: A parameter (value: 8.54858e-6) used to relate motor velocity to thrust.

nodes.label: Motor Velocity (min/max)
nodes.content: The minimum and maximum rotational velocity of the motors, used in the normalization formula.

nodes.label: Normalized thrust is normalized motor velocity
nodes.content: The setpoint for 'thrust' is actually normalized motor velocity, calculated as: thrust_normalized = (sqrt(thrust/motor_constant)-min_motor_vel)/(max_motor_vel-min_motor_vel)

nodes.label: Method for Normalizing Torque
nodes.content: Torque can be normalized by first calculating the maximum possible torque in roll, pitch, and yaw using the quadrotor's geometry and its minimum/maximum thrust capabilities.

nodes.label: CPU Load as Cause for Instability
nodes.content: A potential cause for control instability in SITL is high CPU load, which can prevent the simulation from running smoothly, rather than sensor noise.

solved from my end.
There is a dataref called engine location: sim/flightmodel2/engines/location_x_mtr,
sim/flightmodel2/engines/location_y_mtr,sim/flightmodel2/engines/location_z_mtr,
which tells the location of engine in OPENGL environment coordinate (EAST, UP, SOUTH). just convert it into px4 NED coordinate system. [NED North (X) = -OGL South (Z) // NED East (Y) = OGL East (X) // NED Down (Z) = -OGL Up (Y) (REFERENCE FROM Alireza Ghaderi-XPLANETOPX4 XPLANE PLUGIN SOURCE CODE)]. And it worked…

Regular expressions in makefiles

nodes.label: Regular expressions in makefiles
nodes.content: A thread where a user is confused about the syntax of two regular expressions used with the `sed` command inside a makefile for the PX4 framework.

nodes.label: Post by andy27182
nodes.content:
Hi, I am learning about the px4 framework. When reading the makefile, there are two regular expressions in it that make me a little confused.

RESULT = $(shell [ -f .github/workflows/compile_${1}.yml ] && cat .github/workflows/compile_${1}.yml | sed -E 's|[[:space:]]+(.*),|check_\1|g' | grep check_${2})

j := $(shell ps T | sed -n 's|.*$(MAKE_PID).*$(MAKE).* \(-j\|--jobs\) *\([0-9][0-9]*\).*|\2|p')

My question is:
1. I studied the `sed` command on google, and learned that the `sed` command uses `\` separator in script to separate different parts such as: `s\xxxx\xxxxx\g`. But in the first expression, it uses `|`.
2. In the second expression, the ragular expression uses `\( xxx \)` as the capture group brackets instead of `(xxxx)`

When I run `make xxx`, it works well. That makes me confused.
I run `make -j16 -n`, `j` is null. So I changed the expression as:
`$(shell ps T | sed -r -n 's|.*$(MAKE_PID).*$(MAKE).* (-j\|--jobs) *([0-9][0-9]*).*|\2|p')")`
The result changed to 16.

graphs.title: Why SITL and HITL HIL message receivers are separated

nodes.label: Why SITL and HITL HIL message receivers are separated
nodes.content: A discussion about the architectural differences in how PX4 handles MAVLink messages from a simulator in Software-In-The-Loop (SITL) versus Hardware-In-The-Loop (HITL) modes.

nodes.label: Post by junwoo0914
nodes.content: The user asks why SITL and HITL use different modules (SimulatorMavlink.cpp vs mavlink_receiver.cpp) and different communication protocols (TCP vs Serial) for simulator interaction. They question the choice of TCP over UDP for SITL and the need for a dedicated simulator module.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: This post provides answers to the questions. It explains that TCP is used for SITL to ensure reliable, ordered message delivery required for lockstep simulation. It also states that the separation of modules is a legacy design choice that is now useful for isolating simulator-specific functionality.

nodes.label: SITL (Software In The Loop)
nodes.content: A simulation mode where the PX4 flight stack runs on a host computer, communicating with a simulator.

nodes.label: HITL (Hardware In The Loop)
nodes.content: A simulation mode where the PX4 flight stack runs on real hardware, but sensor data comes from a simulator.

nodes.label: SimulatorMavlink.cpp
nodes.content: The PX4 module used in SITL builds to handle MAVLink messages from the simulator, typically over a TCP connection.

nodes.label: mavlink_receiver.cpp
nodes.content: The standard PX4 module used in hardware builds (including HIL mode) to handle MAVLink messages from various sources, including simulators via a serial port.

nodes.label: TCP Protocol
nodes.content: Transmission Control Protocol, a connection-oriented communication protocol that ensures messages arrive in order and exactly once.

nodes.label: UDP Protocol
nodes.content: User Datagram Protocol, a connectionless communication protocol that is faster but does not guarantee message delivery or order.

nodes.label: Serial Port
nodes.content: The communication interface (e.g., /dev/ttyACM0) used in HITL mode to connect the flight controller hardware to the simulator.

nodes.label: Lockstep Simulation
nodes.content: A simulation synchronization mechanism where the simulator and the flight stack advance in synchronized time steps, requiring reliable and ordered message delivery.

nodes.label: TCP is used for SITL to ensure reliable lockstep simulation.
nodes.content: TCP is necessary for SITL because lockstep simulation requires that all messages arrive exactly once and in the correct order, which TCP guarantees.

nodes.label: Separate modules are a legacy design, but useful for simulator-specific functionality.
nodes.content: The use of a dedicated SimulatorMavlink.cpp for SITL is a historical design choice. However, it remains useful for implementing simulator-specific features without affecting the standard mavlink_receiver.cpp.

graphs.title: FW position controller offboard control with PX4-messages and ROS2

nodes.label: FW position controller offboard control with PX4-messages and ROS2
nodes.content: A thread discussing how to control a fixed-wing (FW) VTOL aircraft in offboard mode using ROS2 and PX4-messages, specifically after transitioning from multicopter mode.

nodes.label: Post by panos.p
nodes.content: Hello, I am running a simulation with PX4-1.14 SIL. My aircraft is a VTOL. I switch to offboard mode and take off as MC. At a certain altitude the aircraft transitions to FW and a ‘‘trajectory_setpoint’’ message is sent to the PX4 with a 3D target point to go to. I use ROS2 and DDS to communicate with PX4. From data logs analysis i observed that when the transition to FW is finished, the throttle goes to zero and the aircraft looses altitude and crashes to the ground. It seems like the '‘trajectory_setpoint’ message doesn’t have any effect - it never reaches the FW position controller. My question is how is it possible to command a FW aircraft to move towards (or to) a 3D point in space using ROS2 and PX4-messages, and the PX4 position controller? In the PX4 user guide I found that only with a MAVLink command can do this: SET_POSITION_TARGET_LOCAL_NED. Is there any way to avoid using MAVLink and stick with ROS2 and PX4-messages?

nodes.label: Post by gabedavid
nodes.content: If you use TrajectorySetpoint you should be able to send velocities and positions, alsong with accelerations if you want. If you use VehicleCommand you can also easily send mavlink commands without diving into mavlink that deep. Would you mind sharing the logic to transition? I am currently working on transistioning the VTOL and it doesnt seem to be working. The command is being sent but it is not transitioning.

graphs.title: Battery_Status messages come in pairs - one with correct values and one with V=0 and I=0 (but same ID field)

nodes.label: Battery_Status messages come in pairs
nodes.content: A thread discussing why BATTERY_STATUS messages are sent in pairs, with one message containing incorrect zero values for voltage and current, but sharing the same ID as the correct message.

nodes.label: Post by poli0048 describing paired BATTERY_STATUS messages
nodes.content:
Battery_Status messages seem to be sent in pairs from my Holybro PixHawk 6x running PX4 V1.14. I get one with ID=0, V=0, and I=0 and then immediately I get a second message with ID=0, but then with correct V and I values. I can see in the QGC MAVLINK Inspector that I am actually getting a pair of messages since the message counter increments by 2 about once every second. If I graph, for instance, the current value it looks like a sawtooth pattern because it jumps between 0 and the actual value on each update. I see essentially the same behavior with my own MAVSDK-based software… two battery updates always come in back-to-back with the same ID field, but one has V=0 and I=NaN. I can try to catch and ignore the bad packet, but I would rather get to the bottom of why this is happening in the first place.

Looking at my power configuration, I have Bat1 configured (12S setup) and I use a Holybro PM02D high-voltage power module for monitoring. I have Bat2 set to 0 cells and source is set to Disabled, which as far as I can tell is correct.

Is this some kind of configuration issue? If the ID fields were different I would have figured that this was the cause, but since the ID fields are the same it kind of looks like a bug. Anyone have any thoughts on what might be going on?

nodes.content: A discussion about hexarotor motors continuing to spin at a low speed after a flight termination command is issued, specifically when using the OneShot protocol on the I/O (MAIN) ports.

nodes.label: Post by SAlex24
nodes.content: I have a hexarotor and used flight termination. A slight problem I always had with this, is that after flight termination, the motors kept spinning at a very low speed, even below the set minimum level. I have the following PWM values for my motors: Disarmed: 1000, Minimum: 1100, Maximum: 1900. So far I tried a few things, like different failsafe values for the motors. But even values of 900, 0 or even -1 (so disabled) don’t resolve the problem.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: Can you share a logfile from boot to shutdown (using SDLOG_MODE).

nodes.label: Post by SAlex24
nodes.content: Here is a logfile. All motors have -1 as failsafe value (so disabled). I use OneShot for all of them.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: It looks like the motor values just “get stuck” at some value. I wonder if this is a Oneshot specific problem, or general. Have you tried with PWM? If it works correctly with PWM, then we have to have a closer look at the oneshot driver. And is this on FMU or IO ports?

nodes.label: Post by SAlex24
nodes.content: Motors are connected to the I/O ports.

nodes.label: Post by SAlex24
nodes.content: I just had some time to do a test with PWM 400 Hz. The motors fully stopped as I’d expect them to. Another thing I observed during previous tests, which might be useful, is that if I activate the kill switch and attitude failure triggers after that, the motors spin like in the video. So the failsafe overrides the kill switch in that case.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: It sounds like the oneshot driver doesn’t implement the termination behavior correctly.

nodes.label: Post by bkueng

nodes.content: Hello, I would like to use my custom world in a simulation. With ROS1 and mavros is straightforward and I can do it, but how can I do it with `make px4_sitl_default gazebo-classic`?
