nodes.label: Post by R_mcc: Solution for Gazebo (Gz)
nodes.content: According to the documentation on adding new worlds and models, all you should need is to add the sdf to the gz worlds directory. No need to modify a cmake file like with gazebo-classic. You may need to specify the world using the environment variable PX4_GZ_WORLD in your make command. For example: `PX4_GZ_WORLD=custom make px4_sitl gz_x500`. Though it seems `make px4_sitl gz_x500_custom` should also work.

I also went through few discussions in which control allocation matrices are being used to send the torque and thrust commands to control the motors directly but I’m not sure how to approach this method. Can anyone suggest me how to proceed with this issue?

graphs.title: VTOL does not transition in Mission Mode

nodes.label: VTOL does not transition in Mission Mode
nodes.content: A user with a custom VTOL reports that the vehicle sometimes fails to transition to forward flight when in Mission Mode. It takes off and hovers, requiring a manual transition via a switch.

nodes.label: Post by Raphael_PK describing the initial problem
nodes.content:
Hi
I have custom VTOL and transition test and flight test has been done but, after some flights, the VTOL does not transition in Mission Mode.

It just take off and stay in the air so, we made a transition through Transition switch with flight mode change. It happens sometimes and I do not know why.
Do you have any suggestions?
I just set the transition heading as default.

I can share the log file but, in this forum I could not find attaching menu.

nodes.label: Post by Jaeyoung-Lim suggesting a possible cause
nodes.content:
@Raphael_PK Could it be that it is continuing the previous mission, and not restarting the mission from scratch?

You can upload the flight log to review.px4.io and link the flight log here

nodes.label: Post by sfuhrer providing analysis and solutions
nodes.content:
Thanks for the plan file. I’ve tried multiple times to reproduce with your plan and the same sofware version that you use, so far without success.
It looks like it’s some issue with the “align heading before transition” step. You could try if disabling weather vane helps (WV_EN = 0), or increasing MIS_YAW_ERR to 30 or more.
Also I would recommend you to update to PX4 1.14.

nodes.label: Post by Raphael_PK confirming heading issue
nodes.content:
Thank you, sfuhrer.
I remember that, at the time, heading direction between aircraft and mission route was quite different.
OK I will try do that.

nodes.label: Multicopter SITL not receiving ROS2 messages
nodes.content: A user is experiencing issues with a multi-vehicle PX4 SITL simulation where the drones do not respond to ROS2 messages, unlike in a single-vehicle setup. The investigation reveals issues with preflight checks, sensor simulation, and ultimately a DDS configuration problem.

nodes.label: Initial problem description of multi-copter simulation failure
nodes.content: User slim71 describes a project to simulate multiple copters. A single vehicle simulation works correctly, responding to ROS2 commands for offboard mode and hovering. However, in a multi-vehicle setup launched via a bash script, the vehicles do not respond to commands sent to their respective topics, even though the messages appear to be flowing correctly.

nodes.label: Discovery of preflight check failures
nodes.content: The user discovers that when Gazebo is launched separately before PX4 (as done in the script), the PX4 instances fail preflight checks with warnings about missing barometer and EKF2 data, preventing takeoff.

nodes.label: Suggestion to use a ROS2 launch file with delays
nodes.content: User iftahnaf suggests using a ROS2 launch file to manage the startup of all components and adding a delay between launching each PX4 instance to ensure they connect properly to the same Gazebo simulation.

nodes.label: Incorrect solution: enabling barometer simulation
nodes.content: The user reports finding a solution by enabling the barometer sensor simulation parameter (SENS_EN_BAROSIM), which resolved the preflight check failures. This was later found to be a red herring.

nodes.label: Correct solution: enabling vehicle_command_ack topic in DDS
nodes.content: After revisiting the issue, the user identifies the true root cause: the '/fmu/out/vehicle_command_ack' topic was not enabled in the dds_topics.yaml file for the uxrce_dds_client. Enabling this topic allows the simulation to work correctly, implying a 'no ack, no start' policy.

nodes.label: Solution for a separate issue: using Gazebo instead of Gazebo-classic
nodes.content: A different user, mrh, who had a problem with incorrect vehicle_odometry data, found that their issue was resolved by using the 'gazebo' simulator instead of 'gazebo-classic'.

nodes.label: Multicopter SITL not receiving ROS2 messages
nodes.content: A user is experiencing issues with a multi-vehicle SITL simulation where multiple PX4 instances do not respond to ROS2 messages, while a single instance works correctly. The thread explores causes ranging from launch scripts, preflight check failures, sensor simulation parameters, and finally identifies a missing DDS topic configuration as the root cause.

nodes.label: Initial problem description by slim71
nodes.content: Describes the setup for a multi-copter simulation using ROS2 Humble, Gazebo 7, and a forked PX4. A single drone simulation works fine with offboard control, but a multi-vehicle setup launched via a bash script fails to respond to ROS2 commands, even though messages appear on the correct topics. The user asks about the correctness of using the '-i <x>' flag for setting MAV_SYS_ID and how to get verbose logs.

nodes.label: Discovery of Preflight Check Failures
nodes.content: The user finds that when Gazebo is launched separately before the PX4 instances, preflight checks fail with warnings about a missing barometer and EKF2 data. This prevents the vehicle from being ready for takeoff.

nodes.label: Suggestion for ROS2 Launch file with delay
nodes.content: Another user suggests using a ROS2 launch file to manage the simulation, providing a Python snippet that includes a sleep delay between launching each PX4 instance to ensure they connect to the same Gazebo world properly.

nodes.label: Incorrect solution: Enabling barometer simulation
nodes.content: The user reports finding a solution by enabling the barometer simulation parameter (SENS_EN_BAROSIM), which resolves the preflight check failures. However, they are unsure why this was necessary only in the scripted multi-vehicle case.

nodes.label: Correct root cause identified: Missing DDS topic
nodes.content: After a long time, the user identifies the true root cause: the '/fmu/out/vehicle_command_ack' topic was not enabled in the 'dds_topics.yaml' file for the uXRCE-DDS client. Adding this topic allows the offboard commands to be acknowledged and executed, following a 'no ack, no start' policy.

graphs.title: What is the difference between GPS and Global Position and Local Position?

nodes.label: What is the difference between GPS and Global Position and Local Position?
nodes.content: A user is confused about the distinction between GPS, Global Position, and Local Position while analyzing SITL.

nodes.label: Post by mhyim
nodes.content: Hello. I’m asking you a question because I’m confused while analyzing SITL. What is the difference between GPS and Global Position and Local Position? Especially, GPS and Global Positon are similar, but they seem to be used a little differently. Thank you for your reply in advance.

nodes.label: Post by oldgazer
nodes.content: GPS stands for Global Positioning System. The term GPS is also used to describe the end user hardware (a GPS system) that is used for navigation based on positional data from GPS satellites. Global Positon is used to describe the physical geographical position of an end user GPS aided system.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: GPS is the “raw” GPS data as provided by the sensor. The global position is the estimate of the EKF2 running and fusing all sensor information including GPS. And the local position is also the estimate of the EKF2 just in the local frame where the estimator is initialized in.

nodes.label: Post by Vacoff
nodes.content: So the local position estimate doesn’t fuse GPS data to EKF2?

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: The EKF uses GPS and other sensors and publishes global and local position estimates. The global and local position estimates are essentially the same, just in different frames and units.

nodes.label: GPS
nodes.content: Stands for Global Positioning System. It refers to the 'raw' data provided by a GPS sensor/hardware, which receives signals from GPS satellites.

nodes.label: Global Position
nodes.content: The estimated physical geographical position of a system. It is not raw data, but an estimate produced by a state estimator like EKF2, which fuses GPS and other sensor information.

nodes.label: Local Position
nodes.content: An estimate from a state estimator like EKF2, representing the system's position in a local frame, relative to where the estimator was initialized. It is the same estimate as the Global Position, but expressed in a different reference frame and units.

nodes.label: SITL
nodes.content: Software-in-the-Loop, a simulation environment mentioned by the user.

nodes.label: EKF2
nodes.content: Extended Kalman Filter 2. A state estimator that fuses sensor data (including GPS) to produce position estimates.

nodes.label: GPS Sensor
nodes.content: The end-user hardware that receives data from GPS satellites and provides raw GPS data.

nodes.label: Distinction between GPS, Global, and Local Position
nodes.content: GPS is the raw sensor data. Global and Local positions are both estimates from the EKF2 state estimator, which fuses GPS with other sensor data. The key difference is the reference frame: Global Position is in a geographical frame (like latitude/longitude), while Local Position is in a local frame relative to the system's starting point.

graphs.title: Px4 multicopter feed forward term in Position Control

nodes.label: Px4 multicopter feed forward term in Position Control
nodes.content: A thread discussing the mathematical and logical reasoning behind using a velocity feed-forward term in PX4's multicopter position control, specifically within the mc_pos_control module.

nodes.label: Post by GHSong
nodes.content: The user is analyzing PositionControl.cpp and asks for a mathematical or logical explanation of why the velocity feed-forward term (_vel_sp) improves position tracking. They also question if _vel_sp originates from the Trajectory Generator.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: Pings another user (@MaEtUgR) for assistance with the question.

nodes.label: Post by Benja
nodes.content: Provides a detailed explanation of why feed-forward improves performance, using a linear ramp trajectory as an example. It explains that a simple P controller requires a position error to generate velocity, causing a tracking lag. Adding a velocity feed-forward term directly commands the desired velocity, allowing the P controller to focus on zeroing out the position error.

nodes.label: Post by GHSong
nodes.content: Thanks user Benja for the helpful explanation.

nodes.label: Feed-forward Control
nodes.content: A control strategy where a pre-computed term, based on the desired setpoint's derivatives (like velocity), is added to the controller's output to improve response and tracking accuracy.

nodes.label: Position Control
nodes.content: The control loop responsible for commanding the drone's velocity to track a desired position setpoint.

nodes.content: The PX4 software module responsible for multicopter position control.

nodes.content: The specific C++ source file within the mc_pos_control module that implements the position control logic.

nodes.label: Trajectory Generator
nodes.content: A component that computes smooth position and velocity setpoints for the position controller to follow.

nodes.label: _vel_sp (Velocity Setpoint)
nodes.content: The desired velocity setpoint for the drone, used as a feed-forward term in the position controller.

nodes.label: Explanation of Feed-Forward Benefit
nodes.content: A P-controller alone requires a position error to generate a velocity command, which leads to a steady-state tracking error for trajectories requiring constant velocity. Adding a velocity feed-forward term (v_x = P*(p_x,d - p_x) + v_x,d) directly commands the required velocity, allowing the P-controller to correct for minor position deviations, thus eliminating the tracking lag.

nodes.content: Hi, I’m quite new to px4, may I ask question about support to less common airframe please? Specifically, I’m planning on an airframe that looks like modified Y3: two main big (12in prop) rotors on the two sides, spinning opposite direction, one small (3in or so) prop at the tail for pitching torque, no pitching mechanism for the  two main rotors, unlike common bicoptors. will px4 support this structure? or will I be able to somehow modify an existing airframe config?

nodes.content: Just a bit more info: I see one common design for Y-3 coptors is having a servo-actuated rudder below the tail rotor, to counteract the yaw-axis imbalance created by odd number of main rotors, as well as provide additional yawing torque; I’m hoping that, by using a significantly smaller propeller for the tail (purely for pitching torque and no lift needed from it), the yaw axis would not have much unbanlancee torque. Of course I could also mount it at an slanted angle to have natural counteracting thrust against turning. I’m mainly concerned about firmware not suppoorting it, but I believe the physics nature of this structure is possible to work with.

nodes.content:
Hello, Good day!
I have a flight controller called Cuav V5+ that has three accelerometer sensors. These three sensors work redundantly and all three are connected to SPI1. In the same way that they are common in MISO, MOSI, and CLK Pins, but they are different in CS Pins. The question that has come to me is how these three sensors are redundant. I read the sensors file in the PX4-Autopilot firmware folder to some extent. But the codes was very complicated and I did not understand much. Do the performance of these three sensors follow the voting logic? I came to the conclusion from studying the logic of triple voting that if all three sensors get the same data, the same data is used as the criterion. If one of the sensors gets a different data, that sensor is blocked and the data of the other two sensors are averaged, and if all three sensors display different numbers, the average is made between the numbers of all three. Is my reasoning correct or is the story more complicated than these words?
Thanks in advance!

nodes.label: Post by luky describing the initial problem
nodes.content:
Hello,
today I updated my system via sudo apt upgrade and since then my px4-SITL stopped working.
Everytime I get this as an outcome: ... ERROR [gz_bridge] timed out waiting for clock message ... I tried making clean build of px4 and I also tried deleting the whole git clone and creating new one + of course running ubuntu.sh script.
Does anyone has idea, what is going on?

nodes.label: Post by Theotime_Balaguer providing potential solutions
nodes.content:
Hi, yesterday had this issue and I think it was a ghost process of Gazebo that didn’t closed properly… I tried `pkill -9 ruby` and it worked again.
Gazebo must be *running* for the gz_bridge to connect, so you could also make sure that the clock of gazebo is running by looking at the Gazebo UI, bottom right.
One last though would be to check that `GZ_IP` and `GZ_PARTITION` env. variables are not set (you can `unset GZ_IP` for example).

nodes.label: Problem: Digital and Analog Power Data Conflict
nodes.content: What is a correct way to use a digital power sensor when the FC contains analog power sense pins? If I enable my digital power driver, both the digital driver and the on-board ADC are publishing the voltage values, with analog ADC publishing whatever noise the V_sns or I_sns are picking up.

nodes.label: Solution: Modify board_config.h
nodes.content: For anyone interested: You need to update the “board_config.h” and add “#define BOARD_NUMBER_DIGITAL_BRICKS 2”. This will stop the on-board ADC from publishing the Vsense and Isense values.

VT_ARSP_BLEND is 8m/s, VT_ARSP_TRANS is 14m/s, and the airspeed conditions are not met. This is my flight log.

nodes.label: Post by Jaeyoung-Lim
nodes.content: Are you sure the CG is at the correct position? For me it looks like the vehicle is aerodynamically unstable, since it is trying to aggressively pitch down during transition, but is pitching up. Also it seems that your airspeed measurement is also quite noisy. Make sure your pitot is placed at a favorable place with less interference.

nodes.label: Post by Park_SH
nodes.content: The front motor tilts 45deg when the VTOL toggle with the RC controller during the flight of my aircraft, so the aircraft has an extreme pitch angle, not forward. As far as I understand, when it is tilted at a certain angle through the VTOL toggle, MC Command should have 100% until the VT_ARSP_BLEND condition is satisfied. However, it seems that MC Command and FW Command are blending immediately after toggle. Therefore, the front motor tries to meet the VT_F_TRANS_THR 0.7 condition by tilting, but the rear motor seems to have a pitch due to insufficient MC Command weight. Is it because of lack of thrust?

nodes.label: Post by Ko_Ko

nodes.label: Post by hamishwillee
nodes.content: Explains that default position mode maps stick position to an acceleration setpoint, which can still be jerky with rapid stick movements. Jerk limiting (smooth velocity control) prevents this by creating a smooth acceleration curve. It also confirms that collision prevention currently seems to require the jerk-limited mode.

graphs.title: Which Pixhawk version is best for flying VTOL in higher elevation regions?

nodes.label: Which Pixhawk version is best for flying VTOL in higher elevation regions?

nodes.label: Post by sri_nandan
nodes.content: I am building a normal VTOL as a hobby project. I have heard that VTOL flight would be very tough in higher elevation regions in India. I wanted to fly my VTOL at some higher elevations. I wonder what type of Pixhawk version would be best suitable to this. Would Cube autopilot work? or should I go for CUAV version? Again I think the basic MS4535 pitot tube would not work properly at these high altitude regions because there are chances of icing. So a heated version of the Pitot tube should be used I guess. nodes.label: Post by Karl_Schoelpple
nodes.content: Some of the more recent flight controllers have heated sensor to always provide reliable readings. However, it would probably be necessary to check technical details of the various sensors being used as I believe some are only rated to heights of up to 1000m above sea level. Whilst they probably still work at higher altitudes they may not be reliable. So look for the sensors that a rated for the highest altitude. In regards to Pitot tube: I’m not sure what the options are there in the hobby market. I would be inclined to use fast update GPS instead.

graphs.title: Heading source & Airspeed sensor-less navigation of Fixed Wing - Yaw estimator (EKF-GSF) and Wind Estimator

nodes.label: Heading source & Airspeed sensor-less navigation of Fixed Wing
nodes.content: A thread discussing the challenges and software architecture of navigating a fixed-wing aircraft without a magnetometer or an airspeed sensor, focusing on the interplay between the EKF-GSF Yaw estimator, the Airspeed Selector's Wind Estimator, and the EKF2 wind prediction.

nodes.label: Post by junwoo0914
nodes.content: Initial post outlining the problem of magnetometer-less fixed-wing navigation in the presence of wind. It identifies three key estimators in PX4 (EKF-GSF, Airspeed Selector Wind Estimator, EKF2 Wind Prediction) and questions their interaction, potential for redundancy, and whether the EKF-GSF properly accounts for wind.

nodes.label: Post by bresch
nodes.content: An explanatory post clarifying the roles of the different estimators. It explains that the EKF-GSF estimates heading by matching inertial data with GNSS velocity, making it independent of wind. It also details why the standalone Wind Estimator and EKF2's wind estimation are separate, citing computational cost and the ability to validate individual sensors.

nodes.label: Post by junwoo0914
nodes.content: A follow-up post summarizing the estimation workflow. It identifies a potential issue: EKF2 does not fuse airspeed data derived from 'Ground speed - Wind speed' to prevent a circular dependency. This results in the EKF-GSF using a default airspeed parameter, which could be suboptimal.

nodes.label: Post by sfuhrer
nodes.content: A clarifying post explaining the structure of the Airspeed Selector, which contains Airspeed Validators, each with its own Wind Estimator, for failure detection. It confirms that not fusing the calculated airspeed into EKF2 is intentional because it provides no new information, only reusing data already present in the EKF.

graphs.title: PID tuning for a small Flying Wing (~47 cm wingspan)

nodes.label: PID tuning for a small Flying Wing (~47 cm wingspan)
nodes.content: A thread discussing the process of PID tuning for a small, agile, 47cm wingspan flying wing that exhibits oscillations with default PX4 parameters.

nodes.label: Post by junwoo0914 on PID tuning
nodes.content: The user introduces a small flying wing that shows 5Hz oscillations with default PID gains. An attempt to reduce FF and P gains did not solve the issue. The user asks about the attitude controller time constant (FW_R_TC), the necessity of a D term, and the effectiveness of autotune for such an agile platform.

nodes.label: Post by sfuhrer on FF heavy gains and airspeed
nodes.content: Suggests that default gains are too FF-heavy for an unstable wing and recommends reducing FF and increasing P. Points out the lack of an airspeed sensor, which means PID gains are not being scaled with airspeed, causing issues as control surface effectiveness changes.

nodes.label: Post by junwoo0914 on Airspeed Scaling
nodes.content: The user confirms that wobbling occurs at high speeds and disappears when gliding, linking the problem to the lack of PID scaling with airspeed. Proposes a solution to enable the Airspeed selector module and use 'Groundspeed minus windspeed' for airspeed estimation.

nodes.label: Post by junwoo0914 on flight with no FF gain
nodes.content: Reports on a test flight with zero FF gain, which resulted in the vehicle surpassing its maximum roll rate (FW_R_RMAX) and crashing. The user plans to increase FW_R_RMAX and adjust parameters for the groundspeed-based airspeed estimation.

nodes.label: Post by junwoo0914 on flight with Airspeed Scaling
nodes.content: Confirms that enabling airspeed scaling solved the 'fluttering' issue. However, a new problem emerged: a large, constant error between the rate setpoint and the achieved rate, likely due to an overpowered FF gain. The user plans to decrease FF and increase P gain.

nodes.label: Post by junwoo0914 on testing with only P gain
nodes.content: Describes a series of tests with only P-gains, which resulted in oscillations or the vehicle pitching down and diving. The user concludes that the pitch controller requires an I-term to counteract the vehicle's natural tendency to pitch down.

nodes.content: I am trying to understand what the EKF2_*_DELAY parameters mean and how to determine their correct settings. The best documentation I have been able to find is the “Using the ECL EKF” page where it says: The EKF runs on a delayed ‘fusion time horizon’ to allow for different time delays on each measurement relative to the IMU. nodes.content: A thread discussing a timeout error with gz_bridge after adding a Lidar sensor to a simulation model. The root cause is identified as a race condition between PX4 and Gazebo startup.

nodes.label: Post by SebastienL on 2023-08-01
nodes.content: User reports that since adding a lidar to their model, PX4 fails waiting for a clock message through gz_bridge. Provides error logs and a workaround solution of adding 'sleep 3' before the px4 run command. Also details the software environment.

nodes.label: Post by TanguyTheOtter on 2023-08-03
nodes.content: User reports having the same problem, despite having a related fix for a world name issue already applied.

nodes.label: Post by SebastienL on 2023-08-10
nodes.content: User clarifies the issue is not related to the world name, as it is found correctly. Identifies that the 'gz_bridge start' command is failing.

nodes.label: Post by SebastienL on 2023-08-10
nodes.content: User finds a sleep mechanism in GZBridge.cpp related to ENABLE_LOCKSTEP_SCHEDULER and decides to stick with their own sleep command workaround.

nodes.label: Post by Theotime_Balaguer on 2023-08-11
nodes.content: User explains that the issue is likely a race condition: gz_bridge fails if the simulation is not yet in a 'running' state when PX4 is launched. Suggests a more robust solution using ROS2 launch event handlers.

nodes.label: Post by Benja on 2023-08-11
nodes.content: User suggests an alternative solution: increasing the connection timeout parameter ('sleep_count_limit') directly in the GZBridge.cpp source file.

nodes.label: Post by Theotime_Balaguer on 2023-08-11
nodes.content: User provides a detailed explanation and a full ROS2 launch file example for their solution using an OnProcessIO event handler to start PX4 only after the simulator is ready.

nodes.label: Post by slim71 on 2023-10-01
nodes.content: User confirms that increasing the timeout parameter worked for them.

graphs.title: How a PX4 boots up (bootloader, linker script, initialization)

nodes.label: How a PX4 boots up (bootloader, linker script, initialization)
nodes.content: A thread explaining the boot-up process of PX4 firmware, from the role of the bootloader and linker scripts to the final application initialization.

nodes.label: Post by junwoo0914
nodes.content: A detailed guide on the PX4 startup sequence. It covers the basics of STM32 startup, the role of the linker script (script.ld) in defining memory layout (.text, .bss, .data sections), using the 'bloaty' tool to inspect binaries, the NuttX initialization sequence, the PX4 bootloader's main functions for board setup and handling firmware updates, and the final jump to the main PX4 application.

nodes.label: Post by Bhagyashree_Dhumal1
nodes.content: A user asks for the correct location within the bootloader code to implement a SHA256 hash check for firmware integrity verification.

nodes.label: PX4 Boot Process
nodes.content: The overall sequence of operations from MCU power-on to running the main PX4 application. This involves the STM32 hardware startup, NuttX OS initialization, the PX4 bootloader execution, and finally jumping to the application code.

nodes.label: Linker Script and Memory Layout
nodes.content: The use of a linker script (script.ld) to define the memory map for the firmware on a specific board. It organizes data into sections like .text (code), .data (initialized data), and .bss (uninitialized data).

nodes.label: Firmware Update
nodes.content: The process managed by the bootloader to erase and write new firmware to the flight controller's flash memory, typically initiated via USB or USART connection.

nodes.label: Firmware Integrity Check
nodes.content: The concept of verifying the firmware's authenticity and integrity before execution, for example, by checking its SHA256 hash against a known value.

nodes.label: PX4 Bootloader
nodes.content: A small program that runs on power-up. Its primary roles are to initialize the minimum required hardware, check for firmware update commands, and if none are present, to validate and jump to the main PX4 application.

nodes.label: NuttX RTOS
nodes.content: The real-time operating system that PX4 is based on. The bootloader itself is a minimal NuttX application, and NuttX handles the low-level hardware initialization.

nodes.label: STM32 MCU
nodes.content: A family of microcontrollers from STMicroelectronics that are commonly used in flight controllers running PX4. The post specifically mentions the STM32H7 series.

nodes.label: Matek H743 mini
nodes.content: A specific flight controller board used as a concrete example throughout the guide to illustrate the boot process and file structure.

nodes.label: script.ld
nodes.content: The linker script file that defines the memory layout (FLASH, RAM, SRAM origins and lengths) and sections for a specific hardware target.

nodes.label: .text section
nodes.content: A memory section defined in the linker script that contains the executable code, constants, and vector table, typically stored in FLASH memory.

nodes.label: .bss section
nodes.content: A memory section for un-initialized static and global variables. The bootloader is responsible for zeroing this area in RAM on startup.

nodes.label: .data section
nodes.content: A memory section for initialized static and global variables. The bootloader copies these values from FLASH to RAM on startup.

nodes.label: Bloaty
nodes.content: A size profiler for binaries that can be used to inspect the .elf file and see how data sections are arranged in the final firmware binary.

nodes.label: bootloader_main()
nodes.content: The main entry point function for the bootloader application, as defined by the CONFIG_INIT_ENTRYPOINT parameter in NuttX. It orchestrates the bootloading logic.

nodes.label: bootloader()
nodes.content: A function called by bootloader_main() that implements the firmware update protocol. It listens for commands (like PROTO_CHIP_ERASE) and handles the flashing process.

nodes.label: jump_to_app()
nodes.content: A function that validates the main application firmware stored in flash and, if valid, de-initializes bootloader hardware and jumps to the application's entry point.

nodes.label: px4_init.cpp
nodes.content: A file containing the initialization code for the main PX4 application, which is executed after the bootloader jumps to the app.

nodes.label: SHA256 Implementation
nodes.content: A cryptographic hash function proposed for verifying firmware integrity within the bootloader.

graphs.title: Pixhawk 5x Power Loss

nodes.label: Pixhawk 5x Power Loss
nodes.content: A thread discussing a Pixhawk 5x flight controller losing power, initially after connecting a YRRC telemetry module, but later occurring even without the module connected.

nodes.label: Post by grayf describing the initial problem
nodes.content: I have an issue with my 5x losing power after plugging in a YRRC FPV Radio Telemetry Air Module into the TELEM1 port. The issue is after I power on the Pixhawk and plug in the YRRC module while the FC power is on, the air module green connection light starts blinking and after 5 seconds the FC loses power. The same problem occurs if I have the module plugged in before powering on. I have checked the pins inside the port, and even tried TELEM2 and 3, the same problem occurs. I have tested 2 of my Wi-Fi modules and the same thing happens, rapid light blinking and power loss. About 5 minutes before this issue started happening, I swapped the RX & TX cables so it would connect to QGC. After I swapped the cables, it successfully connected to QGC and I powered off. After powering back on, this problem started occurring. And about a week before this exact setup was making a test flight but lost control and crashed. No visible damage to the battery, FC, or YRRC module.

nodes.label: Post by Igor_Misic suggesting a cause
nodes.content: Did you try to power it from the external power supply? Maybe it just draws too much current.

nodes.label: Post by grayf acknowledging the suggestion
nodes.content: I have not, I will try that next. I just don’t understand why it would work with this setup one day and not the next, without any changes.

nodes.label: Post by grayf with an update on the issue
nodes.content: Update. Went back and tried to power on, and it worked. Disconnected and adjusted my frame. Plugged back in and same issue. But more interesting, I left the YRRC module unplugged and tried to power on and the FC lost power after about 5 seconds. The ESC still has power so I believe it is isolated to the FC. Tried POWER2 and POWER1, both have the same result.

nodes.label: Post by bilalyucel
nodes.content: Hi, If your controller works in simulink environment fine then it should behave the same in the SIL which means you don’t need to tune for a better controller. In addition, Simulink SIL has “Lockstep” logic so your controller and aircraft model wait eachother. Since, I don’t see your models, I can suggest you some advices. Firstly, make sure that you publish “HIL_SENSOR”, “HIL_GPS”, “HEARTBEAT”, “HIL_STATE” messages corretly on your model side. Also, you need to check that you get correct actuator commands from “HIL_ACTUATOR_CONTROL” mavlink message.

nodes.label: Post by Baldacci

Regarding the Actuator command from “HIL_ACTUATOR_CONTROL”, i did some tests and i notice that i miss some commands, i mean is like that the comunication remains stuck: The controller send in 1 CH, via PWM Block for PX4 Autopilots [1500 1600 1700 1600] The model recevied via  “HIL_ACTUATOR_CONTROL”, mavlink message [1500 1500 1500 1600] Is like i miss some data, but i don’t know why. I took the block for the communication port (XCP/IP) directly from the matlab example. I set also the step size at 0.04.

nodes.label: Post by bilalyucel
nodes.content: Hi again, sorry for the late reply I’ve been too busy. The reason why you get different pwm values might be the cmake configuration. Simulink has “px4_sitl_default”. You can check that on Hardware>Hardware Settings>Hardware Implemantation page. px4_sitl_default configuration uses the “iris” drone(Firmware\ROMFS\px4fmu_common\init.d\airframes>10016_3dr_iris) mixer which is quad_w. You can find the mixer in Firmware\ROMFS\px4fmu_common\mixers. So your pwm values might be changed according to this mixer. Now, there are 2 options that you can choose. First, you can edit the mixer file of the Iris. Second, you can change the vehicle model, by edit the sitl_run.sh file which is located Firmware\Tools path. Good luck, Bilal

nodes.label: Thread: Timeout and strange movement when trying to connect gimbal via PWM
nodes.content: A user is experiencing a timeout error and incorrect pitching movement when connecting a Tarot TL3T05 gimbal to a Pixhawk 4 via PWM and controlling it with a MAVSDK script from a Raspberry Pi 4.

nodes.label: Post by blank-supportgis describing the initial problem
nodes.content: I’m trying to connect a Tarot TL3T05 gimbal to a Pixhawk 4. I only need to control the pitch, so I connected the PWM pitch input of the gimbal to the first and last pin of “FMU PWM OUT”. In PX4, I set the MNT_ parameters accordingly. Also, a Raspberry 4 is connected as companion computer via TELEM. Now I got 2 problems: 1. For some reason, the gimbal always tries to pitch down when connected. 2. For testing a gimbal, I usually run the MAVSDK gimbal example, substituting the SITL system address (udp://:14540) with mine (serial:///dev/serial0:921600). Running the example produces a TIMEOUT error on gimbal.set_mode(). This gimbal was already successfully connected to a Pixhawk 6c, so it should be working.

nodes.label: Post by blank-supportgis describing the solutions
nodes.content: The timeout problem seems to be vanished. My RPi has an LTE-module, which couldn’t connect, because I left the antennas off. When I booted with the antennas on, the LTE connection was properly initialized and from that moment on, the gimbal started working. As for the gimbal aiming down: The values PWM_AUX_MIN and PWM_AUX_MAX set the minimum and maximum pulse width. When you send a tilt value in degrees, this value is mapped to the corresponding pulse width. These PWM values are different for various models. Mine was 1100-1900.

nodes.content: Suggests that mixer files are deprecated and recommends moving to PX4 v1.14 to use the control allocation matrix.

graphs.title: Do I need a Flight Controller?

nodes.label: Do I need a Flight Controller?
nodes.content: A thread discussing the necessity of a dedicated flight controller for an autonomous rover project when using a Raspberry Pi with PX4.

nodes.label: Post by Randy_Hearn asking about using RPi with PX4 for a rover
nodes.content: The title kinda says it all. Now that I am retired I have several life goal projects I want to ring to life that all revolve around autonomous vehicles. However, non of these will be flight capable and more rover/security type drones. I know I will need what is commonly referred to as a companion computer, a Raspberry Pi as major decisions will need to be made based on sensor input, which the sensors I need will have to be added and will be more than is commonly used by the basic flight controller. Given the fact that I will be using large servos, motors, ect I am going to be using voltage outside the range of most flight controllers (I assume) and will need to trigger relays and external ESC’s. So I will be using ESP32, Arduino’s and picos where they are needed there and hopefully even controlled/trigger through the main Raspberry pi. So before I dig into PX4 code and not finding a conclusive answer through searches I figured I would ask. So basically can I use the Raspberry pi with PX4, eliminating the default controllers or simply simulating the input into the Pi. And without using Navio2 or PiPilot. And after working 32 years I will answer the questions I know I am already going to get, such as why do you want to do this? What are you doing? Well, honestly the question is simple, why or what it is for is irrelevant :)… EDIT: And if so, which build is best to start with?

nodes.label: Post by Igor_Misic suggesting Raspberry Pi Pico
nodes.content: Hi @Randy_Hearn, nice to see that when people retire there are still sparks to do projects like this. I hope to have the same motivation once in the future. Regarding your question, if PX4 is possible to run at RPi? If you have a look at the supported boards you will see that Raspberry pico is on the list. https://github.com/PX4/PX4-Autopilot/tree/main/boards/raspberrypi/pico I personally never used PX4 on RPi but I don’t see why it shouldn’t work. Here are a couple of cons that are on top of my mind: it will be a bit less real-time since Linux with a monolithic kernel is not meant to work as RTOS but it should not bother you too much since you will not fly with it. you will maybe have an issue with sensors. Not sure how they will all be connected and if all protocols are supported (for sure ESC protocol DShot will not work). If I were you I would select one of the flight controllers to do all vehicle control and I would use RPi for communication and for camera, but that is mostly because I already worked a lot with them, If one of your goals is to learn more about PX4 then give a shot to RPi first.

nodes.label: Post by Randy_Hearn confirming the Pico solution
nodes.content: Man, you just made my day!!! I have been busy reading the documentation and the Pico is not listed, but I had considered using the Pico and in fact already bought one to try out. I did not think about checking the github for updates. So yes, when I said running it on Pi, I was actually thinking I would have to do a custom main board or something. Although I have Beagle Bone Blues as well I am not impressed with them for what I need. I had to take early retirement, 32+ years on the computer took its toll, and I was in Mechanical Design/Standards for Boeing Defense. Now that I have my answer, the Why or what is to build a Security Rover but I have some additional ideas I want to implement involving Sound tracking and other things. The other project is a simple autonomous mower no biggie there but want to reduce the cost on electronics and spend more on the actual mowing portion. But thanks, already starting to look into the Pico.

nodes.label: Teraranger One Integration Issue
nodes.content: A user is experiencing issues integrating a Teraranger One distance sensor with a px4_fmu-v5 flight controller on PX4 firmware 1.14 beta. The sensor is not detected over I2C.

nodes.label: Initial post by fbenti detailing the detection problem
nodes.content:
Hi,
I have a teraranger one distance sensor, and I’m trying to integrate it to a px4_fmu-v5 flight controller. I’m using firmware 1.14 beta.
For the integration I am following this documentation https://docs.px4.io/v1.13/en/sensor/teraranger.html using the teraranger i2c converter. However, it looks like the sensor it is not correctly detected.
Here’s some logs from the terminal when I run `i2cdetect -b 1` and `dmesg`. It says no instance of teraranger is found despite being connected to the I2C A port through the i2c converter

nodes.label: Response by Igor_Misic with troubleshooting steps
nodes.content:
So no I2C device is connected/detected at `-b 1`
Make sure you try other buses as well when connected and disconnected to see if the device shows up.
`i2cdetect -b 0`
`i2cdetect -b 2`
...
There chance that you are looking at the wrong bus. If this is not the case most like it is some issue with the device not receiving power, or it is broken. `i2cdetect` should detect the address of any I2C device that is connected to the bus. If you have any other I2C device try to connect it.

nodes.label: Post by bkearney on roadblock with initializing multiple drones
nodes.content:
I am trying to set up a multiple vehicle controller with ROS noetic using Gazebo, but I have run into a roadblock with initializing multiple drones in simulation. I am using c++ to create the code.

I have modified the the mavros offboard example (MAVROS Offboard control example | PX4 User Guide (v1.12)) to suit my needs up until this point, but I am unable to have multiple drones arm and fly in the same simulation instance.

For starters, the main function looks like this:

int main(int argc, char **argv){  
    waypoint way_point;

    ros::init(argc, argv, "five_move_sim_node");
    
    ros::NodeHandle nh;
  
    ros::Subscriber state_sub = nh.subscribe<mavros_msgs::State>
        ("uav1/mavros/state", 10, state_cb);
    ros::ServiceClient arming_client = nh.serviceClient<mavros_msgs::CommandBool>
        ("uav1/mavros/cmd/arming");
    ros::ServiceClient set_mode_client = nh.serviceClient<mavros_msgs::SetMode>
        ("uav1/mavros/set_mode");

    //the setpoint publishing rate MUST be faster than 2Hz
    ros::Rate rate(20.0);
  
    // wait for FCU connection
    while(ros::ok() && !current_state.connected){
        ros::spinOnce();
        rate.sleep();
    }
    
    mavros_msgs::SetMode offb_set_mode;
    offb_set_mode.request.custom_mode = "OFFBOARD";
  
    mavros_msgs::CommandBool arm_cmd;
    arm_cmd.request.value = true;
  
    ros::Time last_request = ros::Time::now();
    
    while(ros::ok()){
        
        if( current_state.mode != "OFFBOARD" && (ros::Time::now() - last_request > ros::Duration(6.0))){
            if( set_mode_client.call(offb_set_mode) && offb_set_mode.response.mode_sent){
                ROS_INFO("Offboard enabled");
            }
            last_request = ros::Time::now();
        } else {
            if( !current_state.armed && (ros::Time::now() - last_request > ros::Duration(6.0))){
                if( arming_client.call(arm_cmd) && arm_cmd.response.success){
                    ROS_INFO("Vehicle armed");
                }
                last_request = ros::Time::now();
            }
        }
    
        way_point.go_to_skyhome();
  
        ros::spinOnce();
        rate.sleep();
    } 
    return 0;
}

I can swap the ROS topics “uav1/mavros/state” etc with “uav0/mavros/state” but this only arms and flies one drone. I have tried to mimic this code in a function that is called for in main(), but it is never able to arm or offboard the vehicles. This code I have shared works on individual drones, so it is not an issue with the way_point.go_to_skyghome() function that sends setpoint commands. I have also tried to search for the specific instances of “mavros_msgs::SetMode” and “mavros_msgs::CommandBool” but I cannot find any documentation on how to extend these to multiple drones.

I found on the forums a post by user Jaeyoung-Lim GitHub - Jaeyoung-Lim/mavros_swarm: ROS based mav fleet control for swarming but I cannot see any commands that arm the drones.

Is there a better method in c++ to arming and offboarding multiple drones for flight in a single simulation environment? What code should I use instead to arm and offboard the drones?

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: I don’t think you can get nanosecond resolution in the current PX4 NuttX configuration. You have to do some research how to enable it. Look for CONFIG_RTC_HIRES in NuttX documentation. For benchmarking, I’d suggest to do the same thing multiple times and measure microseconds. That’s likely more accurate than fiddling with nanoseconds, because measuring time in nanoseconds is likely going to have overhead.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes explaining the source of eph/epv
nodes.content: For uBlox, the value comes from the UBX-NAV-PVT.hAcc field, which is described as 'Horizontal accuracy estimate' in mm. The source code in PX4-GPSDrivers shows this conversion: _gps_position->eph = static_cast<float>(_buf.payload_rx_nav_pvt.hAcc) * 1e-3f;

graphs.title: Unexpected Yaw on Takeoff

nodes.label: Unexpected Yaw on Takeoff
nodes.content: A user reports that their coax octocopter experiences unexpected yawing during the Auto-Takeoff routine after updating PX4 firmware from v1.12 to v1.13.1. The issue does not occur in manual modes.

nodes.label: Post by DPatrick describing the initial problem
nodes.content:
Hi,
We’re currently flying a coax octocopter on PX4 v1.13.1 with the Pixhawk Cube Orange.
In the past we’ve had no notable or recurrent issues when using Auto-Takeoff, however we’ve noticed that, since updating from v1.12 to v1.13.1 (subjective observation), our drone has begun yawing when using Auto-Takeoff.
This does not happen when taking off manually in Position Control, and if you switch to Position Control whilst the random yawing is happening then it immediately stops. It also doesn’t happen in other similar modes such as Hold or Land, so it seems to be an issue relatively specific to the Takeoff routine.
It is unlikely to be magnetometer interference as we use Dual RTK to provide heading, and we have also moved our magnetometer far away from ESC wires. Additionally, if it was an issue with heading estimation then I’d assume it to happen in any similar flight mode such as Position, Hold or Land.

nodes.label: Post by DPatrick with more log examples
nodes.content: Here are several more examples of bad takeoffs... Where the estimated yaw does not reach the yaw setpoint, the drone didn’t actually throttle up enough to ascend so it could not yaw as it was on the ground. The drone was often then killed.

nodes.content: A particularly bad case happened today with the drone completing 1.5 revolutions before the pilot decided to abort (we try to let it go as long as we’re comfortable to gather data to troubleshoot it).

graphs.title: Spektrum AR8020T with PPM Encoder Signal not working

nodes.label: Spektrum AR8020T with PPM Encoder Signal not working
nodes.content: A thread discussing an issue where a PPM converter is mixing commands from a Spektrum DX8 transmitter, causing incorrect behavior in Mission Planner's radio calibration.

nodes.label: Post by dkridler
nodes.content:
Our PPM converter is mixing commands given by our Spektrum DX8 transmitter. For instance, Channel 1 and Channel 3 are both bound. We would give a yaw command and it would proceed to give both a yaw and roll command inside the radio calibration. If we give a pitch command, the green bar on the pitch, throttle, and Radio 5 would move. I believe this is caused by overlap in the signal being changed by the PPM encoder making Mission Planner interpret it as on several channels. Our configuration is as follows:

Platform: Quad X frame
Transmitter: Spektrum DX8
Receiver: Spektrum AR8020T 8-channel receiver
The 8 servo wires are plugged into the servo rail on the receiver with the power, ground, and signal wire plugged into the “1” spot. After the encoder, it is plugged into the RCIN slot on the Pixhawk.
Flight Controller: Orange Cube with Pixhawk board.

We have attached a Spektrum satellite receiver to the SPKT input, and the commands come in correctly. Also, we have plugged in the ESCs directly to the servo rail on the receiver and the commands come in correctly as well.

Has anyone run into this issue and resolved it? Please advise.

nodes.label: PX4 6C Sensor input
nodes.content: A user is asking how to integrate a capacitive sensor with a PX4 6C controller to interrupt an autonomous mission, but is facing a power issue on the FMU I/O channels.

nodes.label: Post by Caleb_F_Taylor
nodes.content: I’m interested in adding this capacitive sensor to a drone build utilizing a 6C controller. I’m working on integrating it to sense and interrupt an autonomous mission because of low fluid condition while spraying a fluid. Currently I have the issue that my FMU I/O channels don’t output 3.3vDC. Does anyone know why I’d be seeing 1.6vDC on the power pins and If that is indeed where I’d want to land a discrete input?

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: The power pins of the ones switched on should be 5v. Which pins did you check?

nodes.label: Post by Caleb_F_Taylor
nodes.content: Okay I’m using QGC as my ground station. I measured the (+) and (-) points on the FMU PWM out board. To switch those on in QGC, do I need to give the AUX # a function and arm the drone to see the 5vDC? I’ve never seen more than 1.6vDC armed or disarmed with a function specified from what I recall.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: These pins are not meant to provide power, otherwise you can have the case where a servo draws too much current and would make the Pixhawk shut off. Therefore, you need to bring your own power source to this rail. For instance you can use some sort of UBEC or BEC that comes with an ESC.

nodes.label: Post by Caleb_F_Taylor
nodes.content: If I power the capacitive sensor separately with 3.3vDC will it trigger that input to be high so I can call it in a code to pause a mission and display a message on the ground station software using MAVSDK?

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: You want to pause a mission? I would use MAVLink (or MAVSDK) and send the command to change the flight mode to loiter.

nodes.label: Post by Caleb_F_Taylor
nodes.content: Yes that is correct. I’d like to pause the mission and loiter until the operator acknowledges this and returns the drone to the landing site so the mission can be resumed after a low fluid state is resolved. Does that seem doable in MAVSDK?

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: Yes, use mission->pause_mission which essentially switches to Hold/Loiter flight mode.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: In my opinion if you want to develop using the UAV toolbox in MATLAB then it’s probably best to stick to that system and do the simulation there. I’m not sure how you could also get the Gazebo simulation in the mix as you would eventually have two simulators.

nodes.label: Post by Matteo_Mennea
nodes.content: So do you think is not possible to use Gazebo as simulator with the PX4 toolbox? I want to use gazebo as the unique simulator. I want to use Simulink and the px4 toolbox just because they allow me to design the controller (model based design approach), simulate it and flesh it on the real target. On Simulink in the PX4 toolbox settings, there are 2 different simulators we can choose: jMAVsim and Simulink. I don’t want to use these two simulators, but I want to use Gazebo because it is more realistic than the others. Is it not possible to use this toolchain?

nodes.label: Post by iftahnaf
nodes.content: I was able to connect the PX4 SITL ROS2-Gazebo to my Simulink model through Simulink’s ROS Toolbox. You can use the new XRCE-DDS configuration, this will allow you to see ros2 topics in your Simulink model and send/receive data from the PX4. However, you cannot generate the controller’s code directly to the PX4. You might have to use something like a companion computer running ROS2 + PX4 in OFFBOARD mode.

nodes.label: Post by iftahnaf
nodes.content: Provides a step-by-step procedure for connecting Simulink to PX4 SITL-Gazebo using ROS2. Steps include setting up PX4-ROS2 offboard, generating custom ROS2 messages from px4_msgs, configuring Simulink simulation time, and using ros2/subscribe and ros2/publish blocks. It also details two methods for code generation: generating a standalone ROS2 node or a C++ class to be wrapped in a custom node.

graphs.title: uXRCE-DDS bridge multicast UDP addresses and ports

nodes.label: uXRCE-DDS bridge multicast UDP addresses and ports
nodes.content: A user investigates the multicast UDP addresses and ports used by the uXRCE-DDS bridge in a multi-PX4 SITL setup, leading to a discussion about DDS discovery protocols, Gazebo's transport layer, and a potential bug in the uXRCE-DDS agent's multicast discovery.

nodes.label: Post by Theotime_Balaguer
nodes.content: User is running two PX4 SITL instances with the uXRCE-DDS bridge and observes unexpected multicast traffic on 239.255.0.7. Asks how the agent decided on these addresses and if it's configurable on the PX4 client side.

nodes.label: Post by Benja
nodes.content: Questions the observed DDS discovery address, pointing to documentation that suggests it should be 239.255.0.2, not 239.255.0.1. States that the client can only configure the agent's IP and port.

nodes.label: Post by Theotime_Balaguer
nodes.content: Realizes the unexpected multicast traffic (239.255.0.7) is from the Gazebo simulator, not the uXRCE-DDS bridge. Provides a summary of the correct DDS multicast addresses for discovery and data distribution.

nodes.label: Post by Benja
nodes.content: Follows up on the discrepancy, asking why the standard DDS discovery address (239.255.0.1:7400) is used instead of the one specified in the uXRCE-DDS code (239.255.0.2:7400).

nodes.label: Post by Theotime_Balaguer
nodes.content: Acknowledges the discrepancy and confirms that the address 239.255.0.2:7400 is never used in their system, but cannot explain why.

nodes.label: Post by Benja
nodes.content: Suggests a hypothesis that the agent might not be using the multicast feature at all.

nodes.label: Post by Theotime_Balaguer
nodes.content: Performs further testing in a clean environment using Linux network namespaces. Confirms that even with multiple clients, the agent does not seem to use the expected discovery protocol on 239.255.0.2:7400, suggesting a potential bug.

nodes.label: Issue with uORB message TrajectorySetpoint

nodes.label: Post by Adam_Brown
nodes.content: I am using Uorb messages with ROS2 to make a drone move in gazebo simulation. I am using Trajectoy setpoint to make the drone go up at a certain velocity. However when I assign the velocity it goes to a certain height which is similar to the velocity value I assigned and then just stops going up. Its as if its taking the velocity value as a position value instead.

nodes.label: Post by Benja
nodes.content: Hi @Adam_Brown , if you take a look at the offboard mode documentation you will see that to track a velocity reference you must set position field of the trajectorySetpoint message to NaN. Any other finite value will switch on the position controller. So right now you are asking your drone to go to position 0 0 0 with feedforward velocity [0.0, 0.0, -2.0]. The equilibrium of this is exactly what you are seeing.

nodes.label: Post by dkahle8 about not being able to descend
nodes.content: Hi all, I’ve been troubleshooting an octocopter drone for a course I’m enrolled in, and after figuring out that some of the issues stemmed from PID auto-tune being enabled when it shouldn’t have been, I was able to have a somewhat successful flight after disabling auto-tuning: the drone took off without any issues and was able to stabilize itself in the air. However, when I tried to lower it to the ground, the drone wasn’t getting any lower, and since it wasn’t very high up (and continued to drift away), I brought it down with the kill switch. After reviewing the documentation for Stabilized mode, I read about the MPC_THR_CURVE parameter for the throttle scaling, and noticed the part about how powerful vehicles might have a very low hover throttle, which can lead to more of the thrust being controlled by the top half of the throttle stick than the bottom. Is it safe to say this is why it didn’t seem to respond to my downward movement of the throttle stick, and if so, should I set this parameter to No Rescale? Being honest, this drone has had a few minor crashes while I’ve tried to get it working again, so I’m hesitant to make any changes without really understanding them before trying to fly it again.

nodes.label: Post by Jhiggy on PX4 Vision 1.5

nodes.content: User suggests that if vibrations are low, the issue might be resolved by increasing MPC_XY_VEL_I_ACC or adjusting MPC_XY_VEL_D_ACC for fast oscillations. Recommends using the QGC tuning interface and enabling High rate data in SDLOG_PROFILE for better vibration analysis.

nodes.label: Post by Raptor272
nodes.content: User acknowledges the suggestions, notes that their Herelink setup prevents in-air tuning via QGC, and confirms vibrations are low. They plan to test the suggested VEL_I and VEL_D settings.

nodes.label: Post by bresch
nodes.content: An expert suggests that the issue is likely due to incorrect compensation for apparent flow. The solution proposed is to accurately set the EKF2_OF_POS_Z parameter.

graphs.title: PX4 Mini CAP interfaces

nodes.label: PX4 Mini CAP interfaces
nodes.content: A user asks if the PWM input interfaces on a PX4 mini can be used to capture RC signals from a standard PWM receiver.

nodes.label: Post by szabto
nodes.content: If I understand the documentation well, there are 4 PWM input interfaces on the PX4 mini. Is there a way to use them to capture RC signals from a pwm output of the receiver? I’ve looked up everything on the internet, and tried some settings, but no luck.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: That’s not something that PX4 ever supported. From the beginning which is more than 10 years ago, the decision was to only support (C)PPM input for receivers, or other protocols like DSM or SBUS. It just didn’t seem worth the hassle given the better alternatives existed already. What receiver are you using? Some of them can be jumpered to output PPM (so all channels on one pin).

nodes.label: Post by szabto
nodes.content: Thank you for your answer. I just thought that the CAP/PWM inputs are suitable for this but looks like I was wrong. I have only raw PWM outputs, so I would need to buy a PWM PPM encoder. But instead I’m gonna by another receiver which can handle PPM out of the box.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes
nodes.content: Yes, buying a different receiver should be the way to go. It’s possible in theory (hardware-wise) but there is no code in PX4 for it as far as I’m aware.

graphs.title: Always landing long in SITL, glide-slope intercepted too late?

nodes.label: Always landing long in SITL, glide-slope intercepted too late?
nodes.content: A user's custom airframe in a SITL simulation consistently lands long during autoland. The issue appears to be a delayed descent initiation, where the aircraft flies level for a period after the loiter phase before intercepting the glideslope.

nodes.label: Initial post describing the landing long issue in SITL
nodes.content: A user reports that their custom V-tail taildragger airframe, simulated in SITL with a Simulink-based flight dynamics model and PX4 in WSL2, always lands long. The descent for autoland starts too late. The user verified the glideslope path is achievable by manually creating it with waypoints, which works correctly.

nodes.label: Post identifying the root cause and solution
nodes.content: The user discovered that the PX4 firmware (v1.13.3) was ignoring the glideslope angle set in the QGroundControl mission and instead using the default value from the FW_LND_ANG parameter (5.0 degrees). This caused the aircraft to fly level until it intercepted this steeper-than-intended glideslope.

graphs.title: Multicopter Control Architecture - design choices

nodes.label: Multicopter Control Architecture - design choices
nodes.content: A discussion about the design choices in PX4's multicopter control architecture, specifically regarding controller frequencies and PID structures.

nodes.label: Post by iampete
nodes.content: Asks why angle and rate controllers run at different frequencies (250Hz/1000Hz) while position/velocity controllers run at the same frequency (50Hz). Also questions the use of a P-PID structure for angle/rate controllers instead of PI-PID or PID-PID.

nodes.label: Post by bresch
nodes.content: Provides detailed explanations for the questions about controller frequencies and P-PID structure, citing vehicle dynamics, CPU usage, and the role of integrators in control systems.

nodes.label: Cascaded Control Architecture
nodes.content: A control strategy where outer loops (like position) calculate a setpoint for inner loops (like attitude/rate), with each loop stabilizing different aspects of the vehicle's dynamics.

nodes.label: Angular Rate Controller
nodes.content: The innermost control loop that stabilizes the drone's angular rate. It runs at a very high frequency (e.g., 1000Hz) to control the fastest vehicle dynamics.

nodes.label: Angle Controller
nodes.content: Controls the drone's attitude (angle). It is an outer loop relative to the rate controller and runs at a lower frequency (e.g., 250Hz).

nodes.label: Position & Velocity Controller
nodes.content: The outer control loops that manage the drone's position and velocity. They control the slowest dynamics and run at a much lower frequency (e.g., 50Hz).

nodes.label: Controller Frequencies
nodes.content: The update rates for the different control loops, which are set based on the speed of the dynamics they control (e.g., 1000Hz for rate, 250Hz for angle, 50Hz for position).

nodes.label: P-PID Controller Structure
nodes.content: A specific PID controller implementation where the integrator term is not used in the angle controller, as the integrator in the rate controller is sufficient.

nodes.label: Vehicle Dynamics
nodes.content: The physical response of the drone. Inner loops control fast dynamics (angular rate), while outer loops control slower dynamics (attitude, position).

nodes.label: CPU Usage
nodes.content: A practical constraint that makes it inefficient to run all control loops at the maximum possible frequency.

nodes.label: External Disturbances
nodes.content: Forces such as air drag and wind that the control system must counteract, primarily handled by the integrator term in the PID controller.

nodes.label: Reason for Different Controller Frequencies
nodes.content: Controller frequency must be high enough for the dynamics it controls. The inner rate loop is fast and needs a high frequency to ensure stability and tight tracking. Outer loops control slower dynamics and can run at lower frequencies to save CPU without performance loss.

nodes.label: Reason for P-PID Controller
nodes.content: The integrator in the rate controller is sufficient to eliminate steady-state errors caused by external disturbances. The physical integration from angular rate to attitude means an additional integrator in the angle controller is unnecessary.

nodes.content: I have recently started trying to build a vision based controller for a drone. To test this I have been using the PX4 SITL setup in combination with MAVROS in a Gazebo simulation environment. I would like to pass this as a setpoint to the flight controller, but when I try to do this using the topic /mavros/setpoint_position/local I have noticed that the frame used is actually the ENU fixed frame. I have tried to convert the setpoint from the body frame to this fixed frame using a tf transform but was unsuccesful. Even if I had succeeded in my case it would make much more sense to be able to define position (or even better velocity) setpoints in a body frame that moved with the drone. I have spent quite a while browsing through different forums but have as of yet not been able to find anything that was able to tell me how to do this. I think it should be possible to change the MAV_FRAME parameter to a body frame in the configurations somewhere, but I was also unable to find out how to do this. I am quite new to the PX4 autopilot and MAVLink/MAVROS so I would not be surprised at all if  I am missing something obvious. Thanks for the help!

nodes.content: A user is experiencing issues with USB host ports on a Pixhawk RPi CM4 Baseboard not recognizing any connected devices.

nodes.label: Post by itsDenny describing the USB connection problem
nodes.content: We have a flashed CM4 that works on the raspberry pi baseboard. When installed in the pixhawk baseboard we can’t get either USB host to connect at all. We can VNC in and use the HDMI out but any attempts to connect any dongle or device over USB isn’t seen by the cm4. We have tried to chance the config.txt file to include dr_mode = otg , dtoverlay = dwc2 , otg_mode = 1. I haven’t been able to find any documentation that goes beyond flashing the CM4. The diagram there shows that the USB works through USB OTG. Does anyone know where additional documentation is that would help us to trouble shoot this problem? What settings need to be configured to allow devices to connect over USB Host 1 and 2?

nodes.label: Post by BobWatson providing a solution
nodes.content: I had this same problem. I fixed it by getting a different USB Type C to USB A adapter and different USB hub. I the Type C hub I was using had multiple ports, HDMI, VGA, and a SD card reader and it probably confused it making it not recognize anything connected to it. Once I switched to a simple USB Type C hub, everything worked as expected. The default Raspberry Pi CM4 settings worked for me.

graphs.title: How to change M1 M2 M3 M4 motor pins

nodes.label: How to change M1 M2 M3 M4 motor pins
nodes.content: A user is asking how to remap motor output pins on a PM07 power module because the default pins for Motor 1 and Motor 4 are broken. The thread discusses the solution using the SYS_CTRL_ALLOC parameter in PX4 firmware, configuring the airframe geometry, and determining motor position values.

nodes.label: Initial problem description by Chienthan123
nodes.content: I’m using pixhawk 6c and pm07 power module and airframe F450.I have broken pins M4 and M1 in PM07 representing motor 4 and motor 1, can I use two pins M6,7,8 instead and calibrate it for motor 4 and motor 1? (I am using PX4 firmware version :1.13.3)

nodes.label: Solution provided by DPatrick
nodes.content: If you enable SYS_CTRL_ALLOC (set the parameter to 1) then you should see that a new “Actuators” tab replaces the “Motors” tab in QGC. Here, you can manually define your airframe and map the actuator outputs (Main1-8) to the physical outputs (Motors1-8). For example, if you swapped motor 1 and 4 to pins 6 and 7 respectively, it might look something like: MAIN1: Motor 6, MAIN2: Motor 2, MAIN3: Motor 3, MAIN4: Motor 7.

nodes.label: Follow-up issue: Motors not spinning on arm
nodes.content: I enabled SYS_CTRL_ALLOC and config like u said. when i use actuator testing motor still spins. But, when i arm, the motor doesn’t rotate anymore.

nodes.label: Solution for motors not arming by DPatrick
nodes.content: Ahh, I don’t think you’ve configured the airframe geometry yet! Under the “Actuators Setup” heading there is a dropdown next to “Motors”. Set this to 4. Then set the XY coordinates relative to the flight controller for each motor.

nodes.label: Question about motor XY position values
nodes.content: I have one more questions, what is the value of position X and position Y, im using S500 Generic airframe, i cant find it anywhere, thankyou for helping!!

nodes.label: Answer regarding motor XY position values
nodes.content: On the S500 fuselage, it is advisable to take the center of gravity of the aircraft as a reference and not the FC. By symmetry, I have 17 cm according to x and y.

graphs.title: Simulating multiple physically connected drones in Gazebo

nodes.label: Simulating multiple physically connected drones in Gazebo
nodes.content: A user wants to simulate multiple x500 drones that are physically linked together in Gazebo, but is facing issues connecting PX4 SITL instances to the nested drone models.

nodes.label: Initial problem description by hmer101
nodes.content: User hmer101 describes the main problem: When multiple x500 drones are nested under a parent SDF model to create physical joints, the PX4 SITL instance fails to connect properly. It cannot find sensors like the compass and barometer, preventing the drone from arming, even though the model name is correctly set with PX4_GZ_MODEL_NAME.

nodes.label: Benja identifies topic naming inconsistency and version mismatch
nodes.content: User Benja points out two key issues. First, the user's PX4 version requires Gazebo Garden, not Ignition, which causes a 'timed out waiting for clock message' error. Second, the core problem is an inconsistency in how Gazebo plugins handle topic names for nested models; some plugins use the full nested path, while others (like motor controllers and ground truth pose) use only the child model name.

nodes.label: hmer101 attempts a quick fix in GZBridge
nodes.content: User hmer101 attempts a workaround by modifying GZBridge.cpp to extract the child model name (e.g., 'x500_1') from the full nested name ('connected_group/model/x500_1'). This allows motor commands to work but results in inaccurate position feedback, causing the drone to rise uncontrollably.

nodes.label: hmer101 discovers the root cause and provides the final solution
nodes.content: User hmer101 finds the root cause of the incorrect ground truth feedback: the parent model's pose is relative to the first link nested within it. When the first drone took off, the entire parent model's frame of reference moved with it. The solution is to add a static reference link to the parent model before including any of the drone models.

Hello,
I was exploring possibilities of creating a custom multirotor configuration/geometry and test it with Simulation environment. Basically I want to change motor’s position and mix the control inputs accordingly. May I know which simulation environment can support custom aircraft configuration?
I tried to configure motor position from QGC but no success because my aircraft geometry is lil weird.

In conclusion I just want to know how to introduce a new mutirotor and visualise the data using simulator(for e.g. jmavsim gazebo etc) and QGC.

Any help would be appreciated.

nodes.label: Post by Mr_Madsen
nodes.content:
Hi,

You can do this in Gazebo, but it is not enough to just modify the motors in QGC. You also need to create a corresponding SDF file for the drone, otherwise the Gazebo model won’t react correctly to the control signals. I don’t know if there is a good guide to it somewhere, but the main idea is following this guide and then creating your own sdf file on top of that. For creating the sdf file, I would go take a look at the iris.sdf file and modify it accordingly to what you need.
Hope this helps at least getting in the correct direction.

graphs.title: Ark optical flow with px4 1.13 position hold

nodes.label: Ark optical flow with px4 1.13 position hold
nodes.content: A thread discussing the setup and flight results of an ARK optical flow sensor with PX4 v1.13 for position hold in a GPS-denied environment.

nodes.label: Post by Leo1 summarizing ARK flow setup and flight test
nodes.content:
Report one thread as a summary for the latest optical flow sensor ark in indoor GPS denied environment position hold flight.
Pre-request:

  1. ARK optical flow sensor, follow the instruction to finish the settings, [(ARK Flow | PX4 User Guide))].
  2. no need to enable paw3902 in the px4 setting, even though the ark used this type of sensor.
  3. In QgroundControl, check if the local_position_ned msg is published.

Flight:

  1. I start from stabilized mode, then switch to takeoff mode, it will start takeoff automatically and hover at 1m, the value can be changed, and the default is 2.5m.
  2. during the takeoff, the thrust stick is in the lowest position, and if moves the stick a little, the drone will abort the takeoff. (before it off the ground).
  3. after the drone is off the ground, raise the thrust (pass 30% of the range) it will automatically change to Position mode, now, the operator gains control of the drone.

Results:

  1. no drift in my case, and the z position is very good, the error is < 4cm.
  2. slightly moving or aggressively moving the pitch/roll stick will not engage any movement, it is very safe to flight.

sli

graphs.title: EV data causing the drone to crash when in stabilize mode

nodes.label: EV data causing the drone to crash when in stabilize mode
nodes.content: A thread discussing a bug in PX4 where bad VIO data causes crashes in stabilize mode, which should not be affected by such data.

nodes.label: Post by Semand
nodes.content:
I am flying PX4 v1.11 and v1.13 on the ModalAI Flight core with their VOXL companion computer that gives VIO data - and we experience a bug in PX4 that results in crashes. It’s something that should not happen, and normally does not happen but when it does we need to emergency land or if possible switch to acro mode and then safely make an emergency landing.

So what happens: In stabilize mode when flying the drone, after flying for some time without any troubles, the drone suddenly pitches or rolls in one direction to its maximum angle. Even counter-steering the drone in the other direction only works to some degree, it will still go in that direction. When changing to acro, we can still safely control and land the drone.

Here we have a Log of one instance. You can see the drone is only in stabilize mode, and at the end of the flight, the pilot is at full pitch and rolls to make a safe emergency landing. I have a video of this, and this just happens when hovering, the drone is not at any cruising speed or something. The drone is just scanning something an object from top to bottom.
https://logs.px4.io/plot_app?log=cde7b479-812b-4d3f-8035-c8c79fc4ca3e

The way we solve this problem is when we fly in stabilize mode we change the EKF2_AID_MASK from 280 to 0.

So what we think happens is that the VIO data becomes bad (due to low features or whatever), and think the drone is going in the wrong direction. So the drone wants to counteract this and rolls and pitches in the opposite direction the VIO thinks it’s going to. This is something that would happen in position-hold mode. But here comes the bug, this also happens in modes that “don’t” use the VIO data. We see this happening in modes like stabilize, altitude hold mode, and position failsafe.

How is this possible? And can we switch this off? Or is this a bug that needs to be fixed?

graphs.title: Spektrum compatible vs PPM encoder channel assignment

nodes.label: Spektrum compatible vs PPM encoder channel assignment
nodes.content: A user is facing inconsistent channel assignments between an Orange R820X V2 receiver and a PPM encoder for a Pixhawk 2.4.8 setup.

nodes.label: Post by JohnTarr
nodes.content:
The latest challenge setting up my Pixhawk 2.4.8 Christmas present on the bench is inconsistent channel assignments between my Orange R820X V2 receiver and the PPM encoder I received with the kit. The encoder documentation specifies that the channel assigned to the PPM output for throttle is obligatory on Ch. 3. I can’t swap wires at the encoder without tedious cutting and soldering tiny wires, and I can’t swap channels on the transmitter or receiver.

nodes.label: Offboard mode set velocity not working
nodes.content: A user is experiencing issues with controlling a drone's velocity in offboard mode using ROS2. The drone interprets velocity commands as position setpoints, and yawspeed commands as absolute yaw setpoints.

nodes.label: Initial problem description by elanius
nodes.content: User reports that when setting velocity in offboard mode via ROS2, the drone behaves as if it's receiving position commands. For example, setting a Z velocity of -0.5 causes the drone to stabilize at -0.5m instead of ascending continuously.

nodes.label: Explanation and solution for velocity control
nodes.content: User Benja explains that the position controller module is active if either the velocity or position flag is set in `offboard_control_mode`. To achieve pure velocity control, the position setpoints must be set to 'nan'.

nodes.label: Follow-up problem with yaw and yawspeed
nodes.content: User elanius reports a new issue after fixing the velocity control: setting `yawspeed` causes the drone to turn to an absolute yaw angle instead of rotating continuously.

nodes.label: Solution for yawspeed control
nodes.content: User Benja suggests a solution for continuous yaw control: manually integrate the yawspeed over time by calculating `yaw = yaw + yawspeed * controllerSamplingTime`.

nodes.label: Confirmation of solution
nodes.content: User elanius confirms that the suggested yaw integration method works and the teleoperation code is now functional.
