nodes.label: Post by AS8748 about MSL/AGL from multiple barometers
nodes.content: I have a use case that requires me to get MSL/AGL altitude readings from pressure sensors, and I have a bunch of doubts on this topic. I know the vehicle_air_data message contains the MSL value from pressure sensor (baro_alt_meter) but I was wondering if AGL is also being calculated somewhere. Or if not, what’s the best way to add the functionality to PX4? As for reading these values, looks like the baro_alt_meter is being sent through the HIGHRES_IMU mavlink message. If I want both the MSL and AGL values from the barometer, should I modify this message or would some other message be more appropriate. Another concern I had was, I have multiple instances of barometer in our UAV. However I’ve realized that 1. vehicle_air_data is only being calculated for the first instance of the baro sensor 2. There exist the SCALED_PRESSURE{,_2,_3} messages which are meant to be used for multiple instances of barometers. But these messages don’t include the MSL/AGL values that I need. So, what would be the most appropriate way to solve my issues? Making vehicle_air_data publish for all instances of baro sensors is trivial and I can also repeat the MSL calculations to make it have a, say, baro_alt_relative_meter or something, but I also need to publish these values in a way through multiple message types. I don’t think changing SCALED_PRESSURE* to send altitudes is the right thing to do because they’re only meant to send raw sensor data. Should I just copy the logic for calculating MSL from pressure to my GCS and do it through the SCALED_PRESSURE* messages manually? Sorry for the long-winded question, hope I’m being clear enough and I’d appreciate any response.

nodes.label: Post by ryanjAA defining AGL calculation
nodes.content: For agl iirc it’s just baro alt at any location minus baro alt from takeoff. So it’s relative alt from the takeoff location. It becomes something to manage when flying in mountains or changing atmospheric conditions.

Strange Timestamp Errors in SITL While X-Plane 11 is Running Locally (no Bridge)

nodes.label: Strange Timestamp Errors in SITL While X-Plane 11 is Running Locally (no Bridge)
nodes.content: A user is experiencing timestamp errors in a PX4 SITL environment running on WSL2 when X-Plane 11 is active on the same Windows 11 host, even without any direct connection or bridge software running.

nodes.label: Post by Riley_August describing the initial problem
nodes.content: I’m working on developing a new XPlane 11 bridge for PX4. The individual connectivity works, but when I start XPlane, I immediately start getting imu timestamp and gyro timestamp errors in PX4. PX4 is currently being built with target px4_sitl none. These errors happen immediately on build, I am not starting simulator_mavlink yet. I am running PX4 in a WSL2 Ubuntu instance and XPlane on the same physical host using Windows 11.

nodes.label: Post by Riley_August ruling out UDP issues
nodes.content: Update: I tried it on a VM with no network adapter to see if it was UDP related and it’s 100% not, the errors still occur even if the VM has no network adapter or ability to receive UDP broadcasts from X-Plane.

nodes.label: Post by Riley_August linking the issue to WSL2 runtime
nodes.content: More updates on this issue: it is related to the runtime of the WSL2 instance the PX4 dev environment is running on. The longer it’s running without a “wsl --shutdown” the more this happens. Still only happens when xplane is running, but with no bridge set up or broadcast configured. Seems like a local port conflict of some kind, but I still haven’t found a root cause.

nodes.label: Post by Riley_August confirming the root cause
nodes.content: I have confirmed this is a bug with time desynchronization in WSL2. This is not an issue with PX4’s memory management; just be aware of it when you are working with Windows!

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes

nodes.content: A thread discussing a thrust dropout and subsequent hard kick when a drone switches from Manual to Altitude flight mode.

nodes.label: Initial post describing the thrust dropout issue
nodes.content: Describes the problem: when transitioning from Manual to Altitude flight mode, the thrust momentarily drops out, followed by a hard kick. This causes a non-smooth transition, sagging, high current draw, and mechanical jolts.

nodes.label: Analysis of vehicle_local_position_setpoint message
nodes.content: Further analysis points to the 'vehicle_local_position_setpoint' message. The initial 'acceleration[2]' setpoint is identified as the likely cause, as a large commanded downwards acceleration would lead to a low thrust setpoint.

nodes.label: Post identifying the solution
nodes.content: The issue was resolved on GitHub. The root cause was fixed in a previous pull request (#19162), but the patch was missing from the user's firmware.

nodes.label: Thrust Dropout on Mode Switch
nodes.content: A momentary loss of thrust when switching between flight modes, specifically from Manual to Altitude mode.

nodes.label: Switching from Manual to Altitude Mode
nodes.content: The user action of changing the drone's flight mode from Manual to Altitude, which triggers the issue.

nodes.label: vehicle_local_position_setpoint
nodes.content: A PX4 uORB message that communicates setpoints for local position control, including acceleration and thrust.

nodes.label: acceleration[2] setpoint
nodes.content: The vertical acceleration setpoint (z-axis) in the vehicle_local_position_setpoint message. An incorrect initial value upon mode switch is the root cause of the problem.

nodes.label: thrust[2] setpoint
nodes.content: The vertical thrust setpoint (z-axis) in the vehicle_local_position_setpoint message. Its value drops to near zero as a result of the incorrect acceleration setpoint.

nodes.label: Update firmware with existing patch
nodes.content: The problem is solved by updating the firmware to a version that includes the patch from GitHub pull request #19162, which was missing in the user's build.

nodes.content:
Using v1.13.1:

nodes.label: Post by mtawfiqc
nodes.content: I use docker to communicate with /dev/ttyUSB0

nodes.label: Post by nikolaykuraga
nodes.content:
I have the same output in MAVLink console as @cfrank showed. However baud of 2000000 on /dev/ttyACM0 sometimes is not setted by default on my GNU/Linux distributive side, so I do:
1. Check that things are not properly read from the port; if there’s no or very little output data, then something’s wrong.
$ while : ; do cat /dev/ttyACM0 ; done
2. Set baud manually.
$ stty -F /dev/ttyACM0 2000000
3. Check again; on this step there should be many lines of strange symbols like squares or hieroglyphs.
Also, you cannot use the same USB device with QGC and your own program simultaneously, so you should use additional software like mavproxy.py that provides forking of MAVLink connection by utilizing UDP ports.
$ mavproxy.py --master=/dev/ttyACM0,2000000 --out=localhost:14550 --out=localhost:14551
Now QGC will connect to 14550 UDP port, and you can freely use 14551 port for your purposes.

nodes.label: Post by JulianOes explaining NUC limitations and suggesting a companion computer setup
nodes.content: Not really. The Intel NUC doesn’t have all the sensors required as far as I know. What’s often done though is to use PX4 on an autopilot like a Pixhawk, Cube, or similar and then connect that microcontroller via serial or Ethernet (for some of the newer boards) to the NUC. That way you have a stable/reliable flight controls on the microcontroller and higher level or more CPU intensive software on the NUC.

Offboard mode set velocity not working

nodes.label: Offboard mode set velocity not working
nodes.content: A user is experiencing issues with controlling a drone's velocity in offboard mode, where velocity commands are being interpreted as position commands. A secondary issue with controlling yawspeed is also discussed.

nodes.label: Post by elanius reporting the initial problem
nodes.content: User reports that when trying to set velocity in offboard mode via ROS2, the drone behaves as if it's receiving a position command. For example, setting Z velocity to -0.5 causes the drone to stabilize its position at -0.5m instead of ascending at a constant rate.

nodes.label: Post by Benja explaining the cause and solution
nodes.content: Explains that the position controller module is active for both position and velocity flags in `offboard_control_mode`. To achieve pure velocity control, the position setpoints must be set to `nan`.

nodes.label: Post by elanius confirming solution and reporting new issue
nodes.content: Confirms the velocity control solution works. Reports a new issue where setting `yawspeed` causes the drone to turn to an absolute yaw position and stop, rather than rotating continuously.

nodes.label: Post by Benja proposing a solution for yaw control
nodes.content: Suggests two approaches for the yawspeed issue: either check how position mode implements yawrate control from RC, or manually integrate the yawspeed to calculate and send an updated absolute yaw value in a loop (`yaw = yaw + yawspeed * controllerSamplingTime`).

nodes.label: Post by elanius confirming the final solution
nodes.content: User confirms they implemented the suggested solution for yaw control and their teleoperation code now works.

nodes.label: Yawspeed control acts as absolute yaw control
nodes.content: In offboard mode, sending a yawspeed setpoint causes the drone to rotate to a fixed yaw angle and stop, instead of rotating at a constant rate.

nodes.content: To achieve continuous rotation, the yawspeed must be integrated over time on the companion computer to calculate a new absolute yaw setpoint for each control loop. The formula is `yaw = yaw + yawspeed * controllerSamplingTime`.

graphs.title: Getting MSL and AGL values from barometer reading

nodes.label: Getting MSL and AGL values from barometer reading
nodes.content: A thread discussing how to obtain both Mean Sea Level (MSL) and Above Ground Level (AGL) altitude values from barometer sensor readings within the PX4 ecosystem, especially when dealing with multiple sensors.

nodes.label: Post by AS8748
nodes.content: I have a use case that requires me to get MSL/AGL altitude readings from pressure sensors, and I have a bunch of doubts on this topic. I know the vehicle_air_data message contains the MSL value from pressure sensor (baro_alt_meter) but I was wondering if AGL is also being calculated somewhere. Or if not, what’s the best way to add the functionality to PX4? As for reading these values, looks like the baro_alt_meter is being sent through the HIGHRES_IMU mavlink message. If I want both the MSL and AGL values from the barometer, should I modify this message or would some other message be more appropriate. Another concern I had was, I have multiple instances of barometer in our UAV. However I’ve realized that 1. vehicle_air_data is only being calculated for the first instance of the baro sensor. 2. There exist the SCALED_PRESSURE{,_2,_3} messages which are meant to be used for multiple instances of barometers. But these messages don’t include the MSL/AGL values that I need. So, what would be the most appropriate way to solve my issues? Making vehicle_air_data publish for all instances of baro sensors is trivial and I can also repeat the MSL calculations to make it have a, say, baro_alt_relative_meter or something, but I also need to publish these values in a way through multiple message types. I don’t think changing SCALED_PRESSURE* to send altitudes is the right thing to do because they’re only meant to send raw sensor data. Should I just copy the logic for calculating MSL from pressure to my GCS and do it through the SCALED_PRESSURE* messages manually? Sorry for the long-winded question, hope I’m being clear enough and I’d appreciate any response.

nodes.content: For agl iirc it’s just baro alt at any location minus baro alt from takeoff. So it’s relative alt from the takeoff location. It becomes something to manage when flying in mountains or changing atmospheric conditions.

nodes.label: Vehicle Odometry Z-Position Inversion Issue
nodes.content: A user observes that the 'z position' from 'vehicle_odometry' is negative when the Pixhawk moves to a higher position and positive when it moves lower. The user questions if this is normal and how to handle the conversion to 'nav_msgs/msg/Odometry'.

nodes.label: Initial report of inverted Z-axis in odometry
nodes.content: I am using holybro pixhawk 6c. The chosen airframe is Aion Robotics R1 UGV. The pixhawk is calibrated. I tested the pixhawk with QgroundControl and viewed the odometry data using “listener vehicle_odometry” in the MAVLink console. When I went upstair, the z position was showing negative value. When I went downstair, the value of z position was positive. Is it a normal situation for pixhawk? Should I use negative z position when I am going to convert it from “px4_msgs/msg/VehicleOdometry” to “nav_msgs/msg/Odometry”?

nodes.label: Explanation of coordinate frame difference (NED vs ENU)
nodes.content: It is because “vehicle_odometry” is using NED earth-fixed frame by default and REP-103 (nav_msgs/msg/odometry) is using ENU (East, North, Up) coordinate frame.

nodes.label: Inverted Z-axis in Odometry
nodes.content: The z-axis value from odometry is inverted relative to physical movement (negative for up, positive for down).

nodes.label: Coordinate Frame Mismatch: NED vs ENU
nodes.content: The issue is caused by a difference in coordinate frames. 'vehicle_odometry' uses the NED (North, East, Down) frame, where 'Down' is positive. In contrast, ROS messages like 'nav_msgs/msg/Odometry' typically use the ENU (East, North, Up) frame as per REP-103, where 'Up' is positive.

nodes.label: Post by hamishwillee
nodes.content:
In PX4 you map all flight modes to the one channel. The selection is done in QGC as here: Flight Mode Configuration | PX4 User Guide (main)

Below you can see the screen with mission mode selected (actually on two settings). You could do the same for land.

That is how this is done in main and v1.13. In older versions you could map a channel to a particular mode - but the QGC configuration was hard for users to understand and added little value, so that was removed.

nodes.label: Post by hamishwillee

nodes.label: Post by Bary_Hacohen
nodes.content: The rocketry team at my university is thinking of using a PixHawk as the flight computer for our rocket. We are building this rocket ourselves witha hybrid engine. The expected burntime is 5 seconds and maximum altitude around 1050 meters. We expect a maximum acceleration of 5G. We will not be using the PixHawk for anything except a flight computer and telemetry (no wings, or trajectory adjustment of any sort). Which PixHawk should we use? What we found attractive is the fact that Pixhawk already incorporates some of the sensors we need, as well as even having an easy way to connect telemetry. However, we do have other sensors such as temperature and pressure sensors we’d like to attach, will these be able to also be used on a PixHawk? Lastly, how difiicult will it be to format code to fit the PixHawk system? We are debating whether it may be easier to use a more free source MCU/MPU such as arduino, raspberry Pi, or stm.

nodes.label: Post by Riley_August
nodes.content: The Pixhawk reference implementation has both I2C and CAN to connect sensors, but you are very likely going to need a companion computer of some sort (likely the same device as your telemetry system) to process and send their data to ground control. I don’t have all the datasheets in front of me, but you should be able to find the IMU datasheets for each pixhawk implementation. I’ve had good success with Holybro’s PX6C on our VTOLs, it’s quite a robust piece of hardware. As for code, it depends entirely what kind of code you’re trying to implement, but the pixhawk source isn’t too spaghettified.

nodes.content: So if I were to use the PX6C and would want to use a radio device to transmit telemetry, I’d need another seperate microcontroller? And regarding telemetry, would I need to buy something from HolyBro? Like the SiK Telemetry Radio V3 would be my only option?

nodes.label: PX4 uORB message ID capped at 255
nodes.content: A thread discussing the limitation of uORB message IDs to 255 in PX4, the resulting hardfaults, and the eventual solution.

nodes.label: User encounters uORB ID limit on v1.13.1
nodes.content:
Using v1.13.1:
I’m trying port my code to the newest PX4 version and found that the existing number of uORB IDs is about 231, stored in a uint8_t.  On adding my messages, that number jumped to 270, which no longer fits.  I’ve tried increasing the data type for the ID to a uint16_t in
uORB.h: orb_metadata
uORBTopics.hpp.em:
UORBDeviceMaster.hpp/cpp: _node_exists[][]
logger.h: MSG_ID_INVALID, LoggerSubscription::msg_id, _excluded_optional_topic_ids, _next_topic_id
loggertopics.h: MAX_TOPICS_NUM, excluded_optional_topics_id
and poked at the
microdds_client/utilities.hpp
(Since MAX_TOPICS_NUM sets an array size, I set it to the ORB_TOPICS_COUNT (~270) instead of 65535)
I’m still getting hardfault on boot, triggered by commander.
Does anyone have any other ideas?  I’m currently picking my way through the commander code, hunting for some place where the size of the ORB_ID is assumed to be 8-bit.
Thanks

nodes.label: User provides solution: the cap was removed after v1.14
nodes.content: FYI, anyone coming to this later, the value is no longer capped to 255. This was done in uorb: allow for more than 255 uORB messages by bkueng · Pull Request #21923 · PX4/PX4-Autopilot · GitHub but merged AFTER PX4 v1.14 release candidate (so should be in PX4 v1.15).

nodes.content: Describes the primary issue of the drone's inability to follow setpoints with precision, leading to wobbles and near crashes. Notes a consistent attitude offset between onboard position and visual odometry. nodes.content: Suggests that the onboard controller tuning is poor and recommends lowering rate controller gains. Also points out that the EKF2_EV_DELAY parameter is set to 0, which is impossible, and suggests setting it to around 50ms to account for system latency.

nodes.content: The user provides the answer they found. The max interval for LPE is 0.5 seconds (configurable in local_position_estimator/sensors/vision.cpp) and for EKF2 is 0.2 seconds (defined in ekf2/EKF/common.h).

graphs.title: Random loss of altitude in Position mode

nodes.label: Random loss of altitude in Position mode
nodes.content: A thread discussing a hexacopter randomly losing altitude while flying in Position mode, its unresponsiveness to throttle, and potential causes and solutions.

nodes.label: Post by Themaksiest about altitude loss
nodes.content:
Hi!

I was recently flying my hexacopter (tarot 680 frame) with Pixhawk 4 flight controller (PX4 1.10.1 version). I know the firmware is old, but it was working fine, so I didn’t change it.

Well in the last flight, I was flying 60m high in Position mode, and then the drone started to lose altitude. I tried to increase the throttle, but the altitude did not increase. Luckily There was enough space to maneuver into a clearing, and by that time it seemed that the control was back to normal. At least I managed to land the drone safely.

Here it can be seen, that drone height starts to oscillate, around 5 min, but then stabilizes, afterwards there are some oscillations at first, ant the drone starts losing altitude before 6:40. Drone descended and did not respond to increase in throttle, but in the graph, estimated Z is jumping around by 30m in a span of few seconds.

Here is the log file:
https://logs.px4.io/plot_app?log=70e884ac-7e78-4a06-b60e-c5eb82122ba3

2 things stand out. The “Low on stack” message, that I ether did not notice before or it had just appeared. And the “EKF baro hgt timeout: reset to baro”. What could have caused it? There was practically no wind on the day of the flight. The temperature might have been a little lower than usual ( around 10 degrees C).

Next flight after that, with expensive camera removed seemed fine and controllable:
https://logs.px4.io/plot_app?log=76099b8f-00f7-478f-85ad-ca90bc99d43d

What would be the most reliable way, to keep a steady altitude for a drone in Position mode? GPS RTK maybe? I am open to recommendations, because I would like this no to happen in the future.

nodes.label: Thread: Moment coefficient Only for CW Rotors

nodes.label: Post by CPGHtz
nodes.content: The user asks why only Clockwise (CW) rotors are set with a default moment coefficient (CA_ROTOR{i}_KM) of -0.05 in PX4 airframe configurations, questioning why there isn't an equal and opposite moment for Counter-Clockwise (CCW) rotors.

nodes.label: Post by Benja
nodes.content: Explains that the default value for CA_ROTOR{i}_KM is 0.05 (for CCW rotors), so only the CW rotors need to be explicitly set with the opposite value of -0.05. This results in equal and opposite moments for CW and CCW rotors.

Connection of pixhawk CubeOrange to Nvidia Jetson AGX Orin via PX4-ROS 2 Bridge using UART

nodes.label: Connection of pixhawk CubeOrange to Nvidia Jetson AGX Orin via PX4-ROS 2 Bridge using UART
nodes.content: A user is trying to establish a UART connection between a Pixhawk CubeOrange and an Nvidia Jetson AGX Orin to use the PX4-ROS 2 Bridge, but is facing communication issues.

nodes.label: Post by sebastian-uav2021: Initial Problem Description
nodes.content: The user describes their setup for connecting CubeOrange to Jetson Orin via UART for the PX4-ROS 2 Bridge. They have successfully run the simulation but fail with real hardware. The micrortps_client and micrortps_agent start but do not communicate. When testing with USB, they receive 'Unexpected topic ID' warnings. The user asks several questions about port mapping, configuration parameters, and autostarting the client.

nodes.label: Post by Benja: Solution for Serial Port Configuration
nodes.content: Benja suggests that the issue is incorrect serial port configuration. Advises not to modify `CONFIG_BOARD_SERIAL_GPS2` and to use the board's default port (`/dev/ttyS5`) for the client, while using the correct Jetson port (`/dev/ttyTHS0`) for the agent. Also explains how to use `RTPS_CONFIG` and `SER_GPS2_BAUD` for autostart.

nodes.label: Post by sebastian-uav2021: Progress and New Error
nodes.content: The user confirms the serial port configuration solution worked and the agent now receives data. However, a new persistent error appears: 'Unexpected topic ID ‘27’ to publish'. ROS2 topics are still not being published. The autostart configuration also did not seem to work.

nodes.label: Post by Benja: Diagnosing Version Mismatch
nodes.content: Benja identifies the 'Unexpected topic ID' error as a version mismatch between the micrortps agent and client. The proposed solution is to run `make update_ros2_bridge` in the PX4-Autopilot directory to synchronize the bridge components.

nodes.label: Post by sebastian-uav2021: Failed Attempt to Sync Versions
nodes.content: The user attempts the suggested `make update_ros2_bridge` command and rebuilds the ROS2 workspace, but the 'ID27' warning persists.

nodes.label: Post by Benja: Further Debugging Steps
nodes.content: Benja asks for the source of the PX4-Autopilot repository and suggests cleaning and recompiling the ROS2 workspace. Crucially, asks if the simulation on the development workstation ran without any warnings.

nodes.label: Post by sebastian-uav2021: Clarification on Setup
nodes.content: The user clarifies their setup, including modifications made to install PX4-Autopilot on an arm64 machine. They admit the successful simulation was on a separate workstation, not the Orin, and that the setup on the Orin might be incorrect.

nodes.label: Post by sebastian-uav2021: Cross-Compilation Workflow
nodes.content: The user adds that the firmware is built on a separate Ubuntu workstation and uploaded to the CubeOrange, while the agent runs on the Orin. They believed this separation was acceptable.

nodes.label: Post by Benja: Importance of Matched Versions
nodes.content: Benja confirms the cross-compilation workflow is valid but stresses that the software versions on both machines must be identical. Repeats the key question about whether the simulation on the workstation runs without warnings to isolate the problem.

nodes.label: Post by sebastian-uav2021: Simulation Also Fails
nodes.content: The user tests the simulation on the workstation and discovers it also fails with the same 'Unexpected topic ID' errors ('27' and '16'). This confirms the root problem is a version mismatch in the source code on the development workstation.

nodes.label: Post by Benja: Final Confirmed Solution
nodes.content: Benja confirms the issue is definitively an agent/client mismatch. The solution is to run `make update_ros2_bridge` on the workstation to fix the source code and simulation. Then, the updated ROS2 packages (`px4_ros_com`, `px4_msgs`) must be copied from the workstation to the Orin, and the agent recompiled there to ensure both ends are synchronized.

graphs.title: How is MAV_FRAME_LOCAL_NED interpreted, how to use it in precision landing?

nodes.label: How is MAV_FRAME_LOCAL_NED interpreted, how to use it in precision landing?
nodes.content: A user is asking for clarification on how to use the LANDING_TARGET MAVLink message for precision landing with PX4, specifically regarding the MAV_FRAME_LOCAL_NED coordinate system, and is using MavSDK in Python.

nodes.label: Post by blank-supportgis
nodes.content: User is attempting MAVLink assisted precision landing with an Aruco marker using Python and MavSDK. They are confused about how to provide the LANDING_TARGET message, as PX4 documentation states it only supports MAV_FRAME_LOCAL_NED, which seems counterintuitive for a vision-based system. They also question if yaw can be controlled via the message.

nodes.label: Post by hamishwillee
nodes.content: Explains that the local NED coordinate system is fixed to the earth at the vehicle's home position. Suggests that a companion computer with a vision system would calculate the marker's position in this local frame by using the vehicle's LOCAL_POSITION_NED and the relative position of the marker, and then send this in the LANDING_TARGET message.

nodes.label: Post by dakejahl
nodes.content: Acknowledges the Landing Target Protocol is confusing and the LOCAL_NED requirement is unnecessary. Proposes a workaround using the 'sitl irlock hack codepath' where only the angle_x and angle_y fields of the LANDING_TARGET message are used. This requires enabling the landing_target_estimator module in PX4.

nodes.label: Post by blank-supportgis
nodes.content: Confirms understanding of the angle-based workaround but raises a new issue: MavSDK does not support sending LANDING_TARGET messages. Mentions DroneKit and ROS as alternatives but finds them unsuitable.

nodes.label: Post by dakejahl
nodes.content: Clarifies the two code paths in PX4 for handling LANDING_TARGET messages: one using x/y/z in MAV_FRAME_LOCAL_NED, and the other using angle_x/angle_y which activates the landing_target_estimator. Suggests using pymavlink as a Python alternative to MavSDK for sending the required message.

nodes.label: Post by AngelAlbeniz
nodes.content: Summarizes three potential implementation strategies for a vision-based precision landing system: 1) The 'irlock hack' using angles. 2) Directly publishing to the uORB topic LANDING_TARGET_POSE using a FastDDS Bridge. 3) Modifying PX4 to accept MAV_FRAME_BODY_FRD in the LANDING_TARGET message.

nodes.label: Post by dakejahl
nodes.content: Agrees the 'irlock hack' is the easiest solution. Explains that properly extending the MAVLink protocol is time-consuming. Points to a recent pull request ('Pr land target refactor') that aims to significantly improve the landing_target_estimator.

nodes.label: Post by bkueng announcing a solution

nodes.label: Pusher Throttle Pulsing With VT_FWD_THRUST_EN
nodes.content: A thread discussing an issue where the pusher throttle pulses instead of holding a steady value on a VTOL aircraft when VT_FWD_THRUST_EN is enabled.

nodes.label: Post by Riley_August
nodes.content: PX4 version 1.13, using a Holybro Pixhawk 6X. Everything else on our vtol is beginning to work quite well, but using the pusher for forward thrust has been misbehaving since I started testing it. When the pusher should be activated, it is instead pulsing from the desired throttle and back to in bursts of about 1/10 second. In fixed wing mode the pusher works fine. It also works when set to RC passthrough. The issue occurs at all throttle scale values. Here is a telemetry report from a quick test hop; notice that the actuator control for the VTOL pusher activates, but it pulses rather than holding its value. Running out of ideas for a root cause. I haven’t COMPLETELY ruled out pitch overdamping, but even if I set the min pitch angle to greater than 0, it still pulses, and there’s no evidence of overdamping when I’m not using the pusher. So it definitely doesn’t look likely at all; with VT_FWD_THRUST_EN off, it flies quite well.

nodes.label: Post by sfuhrer
nodes.content: Sounds to a lot like an issue that was fixed in July: https://github.com/PX4/PX4-Autopilot/pull/19865. Could you test if making this small change fixes your problem? PR to include in 1.13: https://github.com/PX4/PX4-Autopilot/pull/20220

nodes.label: Post by Riley_August
nodes.content: Yes, but that cherry pick doesn’t include 6C support, so I went with a nightly build and as of Monday everything is working. Apologies for not posting, we pulled an all nighter getting the demo together for the client. Thanks for the help. I do think clearer communication of board support level issues needs to happen after the fiasco with holybro’s communication and finding information about the state of 6C overall, but that this went well.

nodes.label: Post by tahan094
nodes.content: User is experiencing position corruption (y and z axes) and incorrect yaw when using a MarvelMind system with PX4 v1.13. The MarvelMind data is accurate but gets corrupted after being fused by the EKF. The user lists numerous EKF2 parameter changes made to try and prioritize GPS data over the barometer.

nodes.label: Post by bresch
nodes.content: Suggests the position issue is likely due to an orientation problem, where the IMU and body frame are not aligned correctly. Recommends checking component rotation. For the yaw issue, suggests that the internal magnetometer is unreliable and an external one should be used, preferably with heading fusion.

nodes.label: Post by tahan094
nodes.content: User provides pictures of the setup and asks if it's possible to completely disable IMU compensation to use the raw MarvelMind data. Also asks for clarification on using an external compass from a GPS module via I2C without using the GPS data itself.

nodes.label: Post by bresch
nodes.content: Clarifies that fusing IMU data is necessary for autonomous flight and the issue is likely the magnetometer setup, not the fusion itself. Explains that EKF_MAG_TYPE 'Magnetic Heading' is a fusion method, not an indicator of an external magnetometer, but still recommends an external one for reliability. Confirms that a GPS module's compass can be used via I2C.

nodes.label: Post by tahan094
nodes.content: User agrees to add an external magnetometer and re-test. Asks if sending MarvelMind data as an external vision system via MAVROS would be a better alternative to avoid position estimation.

nodes.label: Post by tahan094
nodes.content: After adding an external magnetometer and recalibrating, the user reports inconsistent results, with one calibration leading to good performance and another to bad performance. Links to logs and parameter diffs are provided.

nodes.content: Another user asks if a solution was ever found for the EKF position corruption issue, as they are facing a similar problem.

Let us explore the list of available (still can be purchased in most of the stores) betaflight-native FCs that can also be flashed with PX4.
Matek: H743-MINI, H743-SLIM

nodes.label: Post by Andreas_Diaz asking about I2C on Diatone FC
nodes.content: Great info! a couple of questions here, well actually just one at the moment. As for the diatone FC, where can you integrate i2c’s like GPS, radio modems…?

nodes.label: Post by Zhengtian_Ma suggesting a solution for I2C
nodes.content: The one that is supported by the master branch is explored by @taileron here https://discuss.px4.io/t/px4-1-12-on-scorpion-80-hd-whoop-w-mamba-f405-mini-mk2. It seems like there is no direct I2C pad available for wiring but maybe can follow how he did to the UART4 by direct soldering to the MCU pins?

nodes.label: Post by taileron providing detailed pinout info for Diatone FC
nodes.content: I2C are TX3 = SCL ; RX3 = SDA (2k2 pullups needed). UART6 RX6 and TX6 can be used directly for GPS. UART4 TX4 (PA00) is the LED pin (for telem radio). RX4 isn´t offered so this has to be soldered directly to PA01 of the F405. In most cases starting Betaflight on time (before PX4 flashing) and carefully read the dumped cli chapter resources gives information about the pinouts.

nodes.content:
Hi,
to evaluate PX4, I built an 7" carbon frame drone.
After setting everything up, I tried autotuning, but the Holybro telemetry radio and the Crossfire receiver had too much intereference with each other, so I switched over to an FrSky R-XSR receiver.
Last time, when clicking “Autotune” in QGroundControl it started to twitch, but drifted too much so I always had to abort to prevent crashing.

nodes.content:
Make sure you have both Multicopter and Fixed Wing autotune modules enabled in your firmware build (didn’t work for me too without the fixed wing part weirdly enough).
Then put it in position mode to avoid the drift and try again. cheers

nodes.content: A thread discussing a drone hovering issue in mission mode, initially thought to be related to a 'navigator low on stack' error.

nodes.label: Post by Hiroaki_FUJIWARA describing the problem
nodes.content:
Firmware：px4 v10
FC : pixhawk2.4.8
It is supposed to fly waypoint using mission mode, but it will hover stationary on the spot until the battery runs out. When I analyzed the log, it showed
“[load mon] navigator low on stack!(204bytes left)”.

nodes.label: Post by Hiroaki_FUJIWARA providing the solution
nodes.content:
The error  message was not the reason why it keeps hovering. (Its just a notification, not a critical error  message.)
It was caused by the specification of mission mode. After changing the parameter “MIS_YAW_TMT” from -0.01 to 20sec. I guess it was a problem about the yaw control when the copter heads to the waypoint.
I am recording this as a reminder for those who have encountered similar problems.

nodes.label: Post by florian.pix asking about non-CAN PWM signal flow
nodes.content:
Pixhawk4 PX4 v.1.13

Starting from the commander.cpp module, where we can arm the drone, actuator controls commands are send to mixer_module.cpp. There they get translated and published to actuator_outputs.

When using CAN this gets than used by uavcan.cpp and esc.cpp.

Where exectly does it go when not using CAN ?

I glanced at PWMOut.cpp, pwm.cpp and px4io.cpp but I can’t find the line where new PWM (AUX) signals actually get set.

nodes.label: Post by florian.pix providing the solution
nodes.content:
PWMOut.cpp, pwm.cpp and px4io.cpp can all be responsible depending on your parameters but when you also want to use CAN on v1.13
you also need to add pwm_out start to e.g. rcS

graphs.title: Pixhawk 1 RTPS Support

nodes.label: Pixhawk 1 RTPS Support
nodes.content: A thread discussing the challenges and solutions for enabling RTPS communication between a Pixhawk 1 (fmu-v2) and ROS2, focusing on memory constraints.

nodes.label: Post by magicbycalvin
nodes.content:
Hey folks,

I have spent the past two weeks struggling with communicating between the Pixhawk 1 flight controller and ROS2. From what I understand, RTPS is what I will want to use since my research lab works on real time motion planning for mobile robots.

I have successfully run the sitl example but am unable to communicate between the physical Pixhawk 1 device (fmu-v2) and my computer. I found a hint on the PX4 documentation suggesting that many modules on the fmu-v2 boards are disabled due to a lack of memory. I am starting to suspect that may be my issue. If so, that is a big problem. Is there any way I can disable other unnecessary modules and compile a custom version with RTPS enabled? Otherwise, is it possible to perform aggressive maneuvers by other means with a companion computer?

Finally, two of the vehicles we are using are an underwater vehicle and a water surface vehicle. Because of this, aggressive maneuvers aren’t necessary and therefore I may be able to properly control them without RTPS. Would you kindly point me in the right direction for making that happen with ROS2?

I have no problem with reading documentation, but there is simply a lot of it to look at and I am not sure where I should be looking to accomplish my goal of controlling a team of autonomous robots (all outfitted with a Pixhawk 1 and companion computer) with ROS2.

Any advice will be much appreciated. Thank you very much for your time!

nodes.label: Post by Benja
nodes.content:
Hi!
First of all, everything I am saying starts with PX4 at commit d7a962b4269d3ca3d2dcae44da7a37177af1d8cd.
As you hinted, fmu-v2 ha the micrortps_client not included by default due to memory constraints.
You can add it interactively running

make px4_fmu-v2 boardconfig

and then navigating inside module to find micrortps_client.

However in my case this led to build failures as too much flash memory was required.
I managed to make it work disabling the mavlink module (again with boardconfig). But I can not guarantee that it will work as I don’t have a fmu-v2 board. Notice also that without mavlink you won’t be able to use QGC or anything else that requires mavlink. Maybe you can find other modules to disable to save flash.

This is my final diff of boards/px4/fmu-v2/default.px4board (where boardconfig acts)

diff --git a/boards/px4/fmu-v2/default.px4board b/boards/px4/fmu-v2/default.px4board
index 22d45c3a5e..f44d2a85c3 100644
--- a/boards/px4/fmu-v2/default.px4board
+++ b/boards/px4/fmu-v2/default.px4board
@@ -27,11 +27,11 @@ CONFIG_MODULES_FLIGHT_MODE_MANAGER=y
 CONFIG_MODULES_LAND_DETECTOR=y
 CONFIG_MODULES_LOGGER=y
 CONFIG_MODULES_MANUAL_CONTROL=y
-CONFIG_MODULES_MAVLINK=y
 CONFIG_MODULES_MC_ATT_CONTROL=y
 CONFIG_MODULES_MC_HOVER_THRUST_ESTIMATOR=y
 CONFIG_MODULES_MC_POS_CONTROL=y
 CONFIG_MODULES_MC_RATE_CONTROL=y
+CONFIG_MODULES_MICRORTPS_BRIDGE=y
 CONFIG_MODULES_NAVIGATOR=y
 CONFIG_MODULES_RC_UPDATE=y
 CONFIG_MODULES_SENSORS=y

nodes.label: Post by magicbycalvin
nodes.content:
Thank you very much for the quick response! I will dig into that and see if I can find some other things to disable. Since I plan on running much of the control code on the companion computer, I might be able to remove enough other modules without needing to remove mavlink.

Should I need to remove mavlink, would I be able to calibrate the board through rtps or some other means?

Thanks again!

nodes.label: PX4 on Crazyflie Bolt 1.1

nodes.content: The user describes their first attempt to get PX4 running on a Crazyflie Bolt 1.1 by modifying the Crazyflie 2.1 port. nodes.content: A user asks the original poster if they were successful in getting PX4 to run on the Bolt.

nodes.label: Post by danfraser: Solution provided
nodes.content: A user provides a detailed solution, explaining that the BMI088 sensor is on SPI2, not SPI1. The post includes the correct code for `spi.cpp`, and instructions for modifying `board.h`, the `defconfig` file, and the `default.px4board` file to enable and use SPI2.

nodes.content: A drone hardware platform which is the focus of the PX4 porting effort.

nodes.content: The Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) sensor on the Crazyflie Bolt 1.1. The central point of the issue is its communication interface.

nodes.label: IMU Interface Change (I2C to SPI)
nodes.content: The core problem stems from the IMU interface changing from I2C (on Crazyflie 2.1) to SPI (on Crazyflie Bolt 1.1).

nodes.label: SPI Bus Misconfiguration
nodes.content: The specific issue was that the IMU was configured on SPI1, but it is physically connected to SPI2 on the hardware.

graphs.title: UAV drifts away when hovering based on optical flow

nodes.label: UAV drifts away when hovering based on optical flow
nodes.content: A user's quadcopter drifts consistently (approx. 1m/min) while hovering using an optical flow sensor in a GPS-denied environment. The drift is fixed in the body frame and persists despite numerous troubleshooting attempts.

nodes.label: Post by knolle on 2022-08-05
nodes.content:
Setup:

  • Quadcopter QAV250 frame
  • Pixhawk 4 mini
  • PX4 software
  • HereFlow optical flow sensor (Here Flow | CubePilot) & PMW3901-Based Flow Sensors | PX4 User Guide (v1.12))
  • Benewake TFmini Rangefinder (Benewake TFmini LiDAR | PX4 Guide (main)))
  • Standard sensors (magnetometer, IMU etc.) but no GPS (due to mission)
    Targeted Mission: UAV hovers at fixed altitude and resists any wind influence, i.e. it holds 3D-position without using GPS

Situation & Issues:
The sensors all work perfectly fine, required topics (e. g. OPTICAL_FLOW_RAD & DISTANCE_SENSOR) can be monitored and show reasonable values, and UAV seems to hold position after takeoff. Altitude is held perfectly over entire flight duration. The problem is, that it still has a slight drift (roughly 1 meter per minute), which is not sufficient for mission target. The log files show that the estimator assumes the drone to oscillate with minor amplitudes around the initial position while the GPS sensor measures a significant drift. The drift direction is fixed in body frame, it is independent of wind direction. The log files also show that the estimator is good when the drone is moving: when manually flown back to its initial position the position shift looks similar recognized by estimator and by GPS (flight path has same shapes, only a GPS offset is given).

Internet research leads to the following results for Troubleshooting:

  1. “Calibrate the sensor.” (usually leads to here: Optical Flow Sensor Testing and Setup — Copter documentation).
    As I am using PX4, not Ardupilot, I could not find a way to perform the calibrations – I could not find a PX4 equivalent for parameters like FLOW_FXSCALER etc. Also, HereFlow setup does not include any calibrations (see link above)

  2. “Exact values for Offset are very important.”
    I used very exact values, but also tried to strongly detune via setting big offset values – the effects of high offsets were too neglegtible to explain the drift by having not exact enough offset values

  3. “The ground surface plays an important role.”
    I performed the tests above an asphalt surface with many features and no elements moving due to downwash / wind in an adequate altitude (ca. 5 m above ground).
    At testing I found the following:
    a. Position offset parameters do barely affect the drift
    b. (Not) including Multi rotor drag fusion in the EKF has no effect on the drift
    c. Enabling UAVCAN_SUB_IMU (using the IMU of the HereFlow Sensor) leads to an instable flight behavior (strong swings / oscillations of the drone in xy-plane around setpoint position).
    d. Recalibration of level horizon had no effect on the drift
    e. PX4Flow roation parameter has no effect when HereFlow is used (as expected)
    f. Slight adjustments to the orientation / attachment of the sensor on the drone show significant effects on the drift
    Changing the pitch angle and the yaw angle of the sensor relatively to the Pixhawk by beveling by clamping thin objects under the sensor’s circuit board affected the drift direction and magnitude. The problem here is that I could not find parameters or calibration methods to compensate for this. Also, even the smallest changes create visible effects on the drift, which is why I can’t imagine that perfect physical alignment is achievable when mounting.

My questions:
I. Is there a way to manually calibrate the sensor / compensate for sensor orientation offsets when used on a PX4 setup?
II. Is there a tutorial or best practice for perfectly mounting the Sensor that has proven to be successful?
III. Can this be solved by adapting the EKF and how can this be achieved?
IV. What is another potential source of error?

Please find some additional information below.
Many thanks in advance for your contribution,
knolle

Add-on: More detailed information:
Here is some more information on the test flights and the log files.
As I can not post enough links in this post, I put the descriptions of setup changes and the links to the logfiles in the feedback section of this flight log:
https://logs.px4.io/plot_app?log=2dc5f9a6-ffe3-41c2-aa91-d591789ddd08
Sorry for the inconvencience.

Here is some additional plots of flight data. If not stated otherwise, the x-axis shows the frames. As the optical flow (OF) sensor has double the frame rate as the GPS sensor, those value ranges resemble the same timespan for both sensors. Positions are given in meters, velocities in m/s. Major position and velocity changes are due to manual inputs to compensate the drift. Unfortunately, number of embedded files to post is limited, but further plots can be provided on request.

Here you can see the drift, and how drift direction turns after the 90 deg yaw:

Shows the drift:

Shows, how the OF-based estimator brings a velocity which results in drift:

nodes.label: Post by knolle on 2022-10-24
nodes.content:
Here’s an update of all what I have tried:

  • (de-)tuning of optical flow sensor’s and rangefinder’s pitch offset (EKF2_RNG_PITCH)

  • (de-)tuning of optical flow sensor’s and rangefinder’s x, y, z offsets (EKF2_RNG_POS_, EKF2OF_POS_)

  • (de-)tuning of optical flow sensor’s and rangefinder’s mounting roll, pitch and yaw

  • (de-)tuning of optical flow sensor’s and rangefinder’s mounting x, y, z

  • (de-)tuning of optical flow’s and rangefinder’s noise, delays, gate size (EKF2_RNG_NOISE, EKF2_RNG_DELAY. EKF2_RNG_GATE)

  • increase and reduction of sensors’ mounting stiffness

  • (un-)tick “optical flow” in EKF2_TERR_MASK

  • (de-)activating COM_HOME_IN_AIR

  • use barometer instead rangefinder as primary height source (EKF2_HGT_MODE)

  • enable & disable EKF2_RNG_AID

  • auto PID tuning

  • manual PID tuning (Velocity, Position)

  • (un-)tick “inhibit IMU bias estimation” and “multi-rotor drag fusion” in EKF2_AID_MASK

  • use “simple control mode” or “acceleration based input” in MPC_POS_MODE

  • setting unused sensor’s EKF2 Delay parameters to zero (EKF2_GPS_DELAY etc.)

  • changed values of EKF2_BCOEF_

  • several sensor recalibrations

  • flying indoor and outdoor

  • different propellers

  • different batteries

  • different lightings

  • use optical flow sensor and rangefinder on different drones of the same model

  • use optical flow sensor and rangefinder on different drone models

None of the actions above brought significant improvement to reduce drift. By replacing the optical flow sensor with another optical flow sensor of the same model the drift direction and intensity changed. This leads to the conclusion that the drift is inherent in the sensor and possibly a lack of production quality.

I found the following related issues:

  • Unstable position hold using px4flow with pixhawk and QGC · Issue #5072 · PX4/PX4-Autopilot · GitHub
  • Drone keeps moving left when in position hold mode with optical flow
  • Reject position control, optical flow, LIDAR v3

Possibly these are solved when you read this searching for solutions.

Best regards,
knolle

nodes.content: A thread discussing a potential bug in the parasite drag formula used in PX4 firmware, where it violates the principle of force decomposition by using velocity components instead of the total airspeed.

nodes.label: Initial post by wangww identifying the bug
nodes.content: The parasite drag formula used by this script (and the Firmware) seems incorrect because it violate the principle of force decomposition. The 'v' in the drag equation should be the total relative airspeed, not the velocity components at each axis.

nodes.label: Confirmation post by bresch
nodes.content: You’re right, the model assumes Drag = Drag_x + Drag_y, which isn’t correct since the drag is a vector.

nodes.label: Explanation post by Paul_Riseborough
nodes.content: The bluff body drag is modelled as a flat plate facing forward and another facing sideways which simplifies the equations but does over estimate the drag in the ‘corners’. The alternative is to do the computation in polar coordinates.

nodes.label: Solution post by bresch
nodes.content: Finally addressed here: EKF2: Improve bluff body drag model by bresch · Pull Request #20848 · PX4/PX4-Autopilot · GitHub

nodes.label: Confirmation of solution by wangww
nodes.content: It looks good! Gladly to see this problem solved! I’ll mark this reply as the solution.

nodes.label: Post by Salvatore Marcellini & Junwoo
nodes.content: Salvatore asks how to implement a custom controller for a tilt-rotor multicopter using a 6D desired vector (forces and moments) and map it to motors and servos. He has already modified the mc_position, mc_attitude, and mc_rate controllers but is stuck on actuator outputs. Junwoo suggests using the new Control Allocation feature.

nodes.label: Post by Junwoo
nodes.content: Junwoo suggests two approaches: 1) Bypass the control_allocator module and publish directly to actuator_motors and actuator_servos topics from a custom module. 2) Use the Control Allocator with a 'Custom' airframe type to map servos and motors.

nodes.label: Post by Salvatore Marcellini
nodes.content: Salvatore expresses concern that bypassing the allocator might disable safety features. He also thinks the 'Custom' airframe solution might not account for the change in thrust vector when a motor is tilted, and asks about the difficulty of creating a new allocator.

nodes.label: Post by Junwoo
nodes.content: Junwoo clarifies that the control allocator is designed to do exactly what is needed: take a 6D force/torque vector and mix it for servos and motors, accounting for geometry like tilt angles.

nodes.label: Post by Salvatore Marcellini
nodes.content: Salvatore questions if the standard multicopter control allocator handles servo tilt angles, expressing confusion on how to integrate his requirements into PX4.

nodes.label: Post by Junwoo
nodes.content: Junwoo confirms the standard multicopter allocator does not handle servos. He advises setting the CA_AIRFRAME parameter to 'CUSTOM' to define the specific geometry.

nodes.label: Post by Junwoo
nodes.content: Junwoo proposes a better solution: setting the CA_AIRFRAME parameter to 'Multirotor with Tilt', which is a pre-supported configuration. He notes a limitation that tilt directions are confined to Front or Right.

nodes.label: Post by Salvatore Marcellini
nodes.content: Salvatore believes the 'Multirotor with Tilt' is for bicopters and not suitable for his X-configuration drone used in his PhD research, which requires tilt for roll, pitch, and yaw control.

nodes.label: Post by Junwoo
nodes.content: Junwoo provides a link to the Control Allocation documentation, specifically pointing to the section on adding a new geometry or output function.

nodes.label: Post by Junwoo
nodes.content: Junwoo provides a code snippet and suggests creating a new geometry class, like 'ActuatorEffectivenessTiltrotorMulticopter', as an advanced solution for direct actuator control.

graphs.title: Failed repeated reading from a file in HITL mode

nodes.label: Failed repeated reading from a file in HITL mode
nodes.content: A user's PX4 module fails to read from a file on the second attempt in HITL mode, receiving an error. The root cause is identified as NuttX's thread-specific file descriptors.

nodes.label: Initial problem report
nodes.content: A custom PX4 module reads 100 bytes from a file. The first read works, but the second call to the 'test' command fails with 'can't read from 3, because 13'. The user suspects an issue with the file descriptor's validity across command calls.

nodes.label: Problem reason found
nodes.content: The user discovered that in NuttX, file descriptors are thread-specific. The 'custom_command' is executed in a new thread each time, so the file descriptor opened in the first call is not valid in the second call's thread.

nodes.label: File I/O Error on Repeated Read

nodes.label: px4_read

nodes.label: custom_command

nodes.label: File descriptors are thread-specific in NuttX

nodes.label: Post by bresch
nodes.content: In the log, the autopilot tries to command a negative roll (i.e.: left bank) while on the video, it seems that the plane tries to do a right turn. Are you sure the motors are wired to the correct outputs? Also, note that the magnetometer is highly influenced by some magnetic field (from the drone or the laptop below it); this will create a heading issue

nodes.label: Post by fastwalker
nodes.content: If, you look at the video when I run the motors using servo tester the plane hovers correctly. In the backyard the plane still behaves the same (left motor high, right motor low, tail motor high). My GPS broke so, at this point I am running without the GPS until the new GPS is delivered. nodes.label: Post by bresch
nodes.content: It doesn’t hover with a servo tester, the motors are just spinning at a constant RPM; this doesn’t tell you if the motors are connected to the correct output. You need to verify that the 'motor right' output is connected to the right motor, 'motor left' to the left motor and so on. How did you modify it? Did you change the mixer to use: R: 3y. Otherwise you could also use the convergence airframe config and modify it to use the elevator.

nodes.label: Post by ben_b (Initial Problem)
nodes.content: The user reports that the mrobotics CAN airspeed sensor is not working on PX4 v1.13.0 (stable or main) on either a Pixhawk 4 or Pixhawk 6X. It previously worked on v1.11 with UAVCAN_ENABLE set to 2. Trying to enable UAVCAN_SUB_ASPD did not resolve the issue.

nodes.label: Post by Abstractless on 2022-07-11
nodes.content: Looking to use PX4_SIM_SPEED_FACTOR on an empty world using gazebo_sitl_multiple_run.sh. My full command is: PX4_SIM_SPEED_FACTOR=5 Tools/gazebo_sitl_multiple_run.sh -mplane -n2. The error I am receiving is: [Err] [gazebo_mavlink_interface.cpp:397] max_step_size of 0.004 s does not match real_time_update_rate of 1250, aborting. Tried compiling with the speed factor first, but the error persists for multiple drones. Manually changing max_step_size was not helpful.

nodes.label: Post by Abstractless on 2022-07-11
nodes.content: Analysis of gazebo_mavlink_interface.cpp reveals that the check for consistency between real_time_update_rate and max_step_size occurs before the update rate is adjusted by the speed factor. For multiple drones, the update rate value accumulates with each new instance, causing the check to fail for the second drone onwards.

nodes.label: Post by mnumanuyar on 2023-02-13
nodes.content: Confirms the issue is still a live bug and references a related GitHub issue and pull request.

nodes.label: Post by Sharan123 on 2023-11-01
nodes.content: Confirms the bug is still active, working for a single UAV but failing for two. Proposes a potential workaround of programmatically changing the real_time_update_rate after the UAVs are spawned.

nodes.content: Using PX4_SIM_SPEED_FACTOR with multiple drones via gazebo_sitl_multiple_run.sh causes a crash. The root cause is in gazebo_mavlink_interface.cpp where a check for physics parameter consistency fails because the real_time_update_rate is cumulatively modified for each drone instance before the check is performed.

graphs.title: Atomic sections via masking global interrupts

nodes.label: Atomic sections via masking global interrupts
nodes.content: A thread discussing how to handle atomic sections and critical sections in a protected build (kernel/userspace) environment, particularly for RISC-V and ARM architectures in PX4.

nodes.label: Post by pussuw on 2022-06-28
nodes.content: Introduces the problem of calling enter_critical_section() from unprivileged mode on RISC-V while implementing a protected build. This causes a system crash. On ARM, the instruction is silently ignored, leading to potential race conditions. Proposes a new 'px4::critical' class as a solution.

nodes.label: Post by bkueng on 2022-08-26
nodes.content: Agrees that a 'px4::critical' abstraction makes sense. Notes that px4::atomic is used from IRQ handlers. Suggests a simpler solution using conditional compilation based on the '__KERNEL__' and 'CONFIG_BUILD_FLAT' flags, letting GCC handle locking in userspace.

nodes.label: Post by pussuw on 2022-09-06
nodes.content: Provides a link to the implemented fix on GitHub, which uses the conditional compilation approach.

nodes.label: Post by pussuw on 2022-09-06
nodes.content: Explains that the 'px4::critical' abstraction was also implemented but discarded because it used almost 6K of flash memory, which is too much for memory-constrained targets. The flagging approach was chosen instead.

nodes.content: The original poster, working on a RISC-V port.

nodes.label: bkueng
nodes.content: A user who provided feedback and an alternative solution.

nodes.label: Protected Build (Kernel/Userspace Separation)
nodes.content: A build mode in NuttX that separates kernel and user space, preventing user applications from accessing privileged resources directly.

nodes.label: Atomic Sections
nodes.content: A block of code that must be executed without interruption to prevent race conditions, typically implemented by masking global interrupts.

nodes.label: Privileged Instruction from Unprivileged Mode
nodes.content: The core issue where code running in userspace attempts to execute an instruction reserved for the kernel, such as disabling interrupts.

nodes.label: NuttX
nodes.content: The real-time operating system used by PX4.

nodes.label: px4::atomic
nodes.content: A PX4 C++ template class for atomic operations which internally uses critical sections.

nodes.label: RISC-V
nodes.content: An open-source instruction set architecture. On this platform, a privilege violation causes a system crash.

nodes.label: ARM
nodes.content: A family of RISC architectures. On this platform, a privileged instruction from userspace is silently ignored, which can lead to hard-to-debug race conditions.

nodes.label: enter_critical_section()
nodes.content: A function/macro that masks global interrupts to begin an atomic section. It is a privileged operation.

nodes.label: Illegal Instruction Crash
nodes.content: A system crash that occurs on RISC-V when a privileged instruction is executed from userspace.

nodes.label: Unprivileged Mode (Userspace)
nodes.content: A restricted execution mode for applications, separate from the kernel.

nodes.label: ISR Context
nodes.content: The execution context of an Interrupt Service Routine (IRQ handler).

nodes.label: Proposed 'px4::critical' class
nodes.content: A proposed abstraction that would use mutexes/semaphores in userspace and direct interrupt masking in kernelspace. It was discarded due to high flash memory usage (6KB).

nodes.label: Conditional Compilation Fix (PR #20170)
nodes.content: The implemented solution that uses preprocessor flags like '__KERNEL__' and 'CONFIG_BUILD_FLAT' to prevent 'enter_critical_section' from being compiled into user-space code.

nodes.label: __KERNEL__

graphs.title: Is PX4Flow output raw data accurate?

nodes.label: Is PX4Flow output raw data accurate?
nodes.content: A thread discussing the accuracy of raw PX4Flow sensor data for indoor drone hovering and how the PX4 flight stack processes this data to achieve stability.

nodes.label: Post by U7777777
nodes.content: User is building a custom FPGA-based drone for indoor hovering. The drone can hold altitude with an ultrasonic sensor but drifts horizontally. The raw optical flow data (flow_x, flow_y) from the PX4Flow sensor seems unstable and sensitive to vibrations. The user asks how PX4 handles this raw data.

nodes.label: Post by bresch
nodes.content: Explains that PX4 compensates for the drone's angular velocity (using gyro data) to clean up the optical flow signal. The result is then fused into the EKF2 (Extended Kalman Filter) to get a stable velocity estimate. Suggests an alternative using a simpler complementary filter if an EKF is not available.

nodes.label: Post by U7777777
nodes.content: User confirms their understanding of the data pipeline: raw flow is scaled by a rangefinder, fed into EKF2 to get a velocity estimate, which is then used by a PID controller to correct drift. Asks how yaw rotation (z-axis drift) is compensated for, as it would also affect the optical flow image.

nodes.label: Post by AlexKlimaj
nodes.content: Confirms that the PX4 optical flow data pipeline compensates for yaw using gyro data. Also suggests an alternative sensor, the ARK Flow.

nodes.label: Post by bresch
nodes.content: Clarifies that yaw compensation is handled by EKF2. If the sensor is not centered on the drone's Z-axis, its position can be specified using EKF2_OF_POS_X/Y/Z parameters, allowing the EKF to correctly compensate for flow generated by yaw rotation.

nodes.label: Post by U7777777
nodes.content: User reiterates their goal is to provide an accurate velocity to their PID system and asks if the VehicleOpticalFlow.cpp file contains all the rotation compensation logic.

nodes.label: Indoor Drone Hovering
nodes.content: The primary goal of the project is to achieve stable drone hovering in an indoor environment without GPS.

nodes.label: Horizontal Drone Drift
nodes.content: The problem where the drone drifts left and right instead of maintaining a fixed position.

nodes.label: Unstable Optical Flow Data
nodes.content: The raw output from the PX4Flow sensor is unstable and highly affected by vibrations, making it difficult to use directly for position control.

nodes.label: Yaw Rotation Compensation
nodes.content: The challenge of correcting optical flow data for the effects of the drone rotating around its vertical (yaw) axis.

nodes.label: PX4Flow Sensor
nodes.content: An optical flow sensor used to measure horizontal velocity (vx, vy) by tracking features on the ground.

nodes.label: Custom FPGA Flight Controller
nodes.content: The user's custom flight controller hardware based on an FPGA, running custom code.

nodes.label: Ultrasonic Sensor
nodes.content: A sensor used for maintaining a constant altitude.

nodes.label: Gyro
nodes.content: A sensor that measures angular velocity, used to compensate for the drone's rotation in the optical flow calculation.

nodes.label: Range Finder
nodes.content: A sensor (like ultrasonic or lidar) that measures distance to the ground, used to scale the optical flow pixel movement into real-world velocity.

nodes.label: ARK Flow Sensor
nodes.content: An alternative optical flow and distance sensor mentioned in the thread.

nodes.label: EKF2 (Extended Kalman Filter)
nodes.content: A software module in PX4 that fuses data from multiple sensors (like optical flow, gyro, accelerometer) to produce a stable estimate of the drone's state, including its velocity.

nodes.label: PID System
nodes.content: A control loop mechanism that uses the estimated velocity to calculate the necessary motor commands to counteract drift and achieve hovering.

nodes.label: VehicleOpticalFlow.cpp
nodes.content: A specific source code file in the PX4 Autopilot repository that handles optical flow data processing.

nodes.label: flow_x and flow_y
nodes.content: The raw optical flow measurements from the PX4Flow sensor representing pixel movement.

nodes.label: Velocity Estimate
nodes.content: The smoothed and corrected velocity of the drone, produced by EKF2, which is used for position control.

nodes.label: EKF2_OF_POS_X/Y/Z
nodes.content: Configuration parameters in PX4 that specify the physical position of the optical flow sensor relative to the drone's center of gravity. This is crucial for accurate yaw compensation.

nodes.label: Gyro Compensation
nodes.content: The technique of using gyro data to subtract the motion caused by the drone's own rotation from the raw optical flow data.

nodes.label: Fusing Optical Flow in EKF2
nodes.content: The process of feeding the compensated optical flow data into an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF2) as an aiding source to generate a robust velocity estimate.

graphs.title: How to send digital sensor data read in STM32 or Arduino to Pixhawk?

nodes.label: How to send digital sensor data read in STM32 or Arduino to Pixhawk?
nodes.content: A thread asking for the method to send digital sensor data from a microcontroller like STM32 or Arduino to a Pixhawk flight controller, and which communication protocol (I2C or USART) to use.

nodes.label: Post by yardimcioyuncu asking for communication method
nodes.content:
Hello everyone,

I am reading digital sensor data with STM32. I want to send this I/O data to Pixhawk Cube Orange. Later I want to show it on my ground station from Pixhawk. How should I go about this? Which I2C or USART should I use?

Kaan IŞIK
Embedded Software Engineer

nodes.label: STM32

nodes.label: Arduino
nodes.content: An open-source electronics platform mentioned as an alternative microcontroller for reading sensor data.

nodes.label: Pixhawk Cube Orange

nodes.label: Digital Sensor

nodes.label: Ground Station

nodes.label: I2C
nodes.content: Inter-Integrated Circuit, a serial communication protocol suggested as a possible method for data transfer.

nodes.label: USART
nodes.content: Universal Synchronous/Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter, a serial communication protocol suggested as a possible method for data transfer.
